text: The French honorific for a bishop, roughly 'My Lord'. Madame Magloire uses it with relish; the Bishop himself prefers the nickname the poor give him. Hapgood sometimes translates it as 'Monsignor' or simply leaves it.
quote: housekeeper to Monseigneur

text: Under the old monarchy a 'parliament' was not a legislature but a sovereign law court. Aix-en-Provence had one, and its councillors formed the 'nobility of the bar' (noblesse de robe), a hereditary caste of judges. M. Myriel was born into that world, which the Revolution destroyed.
quote: the nobility of the bar

text: To emigrate, in a French context, means to have fled the Revolution: the émigrés were the nobles and clergy who left France after 1789, many of them ruined. Returning émigrés, often ruined, were a familiar type under the Restoration.
quote: emigrated to Italy

text: Shorthand for 1793, the year of the Terror: the execution of Louis XVI, the guillotine in permanent session, civil war in the Vendée. For royalists it is the Revolution's unforgivable year; for republicans, a thunderbolt that answered fifteen centuries of oppression.
quote: the tragic spectacles of ’93

text: A parish priest. A curé might be assisted by a vicar (vicaire), and village curés were often poor and little educated. Hugo keeps the French word throughout.
quote: the Curé of Brignolles

text: Joseph Fesch (1763–1839), half-brother of Napoleon's mother and so the Emperor's uncle, Archbishop of Lyons and a cardinal. He was the natural channel for a provincial priest seeking favours in Paris. Hugo's anecdote of the Emperor meeting Myriel in Fesch's anteroom is invented.
quote: M. le Cardinal Fesch

text: Napoleon crowned himself Emperor in Notre-Dame on 2 December 1804, with Pope Pius VII present. The 'epoch of the coronation' is therefore late 1804, when the Empire was new and bishoprics were in the Emperor's gift.
quote: the epoch of the coronation

text: The head of a département, appointed by the central government in Paris, created by Napoleon in 1800. A prefect ran the local administration and police and was the most powerful official in a provincial town, outranking the mayor.
quote: the general and the prefect

text: The livre was the old unit of account, replaced by the franc in 1795 at the same value; old-fashioned people like the Bishop went on reckoning in livres. 15,000 a year was a handsome salary when a labourer earned perhaps 500 francs a year, so the 1,500 the Bishop and his sister keep is genuine poverty.
quote: 15,000 livres

text: Priests of the Congregation of the Mission, founded by Saint Vincent de Paul in 1625 and nicknamed after their Paris house of Saint-Lazare. They preached in the countryside and trained clergy. Vincent also founded the Sisters of Charity, the nursing nuns of French hospitals.
quote: the Lazarists of Montdidier

text: Imprisonment for debt was legal in France until 1867. A creditor could have a debtor locked up, at the creditor's expense, until the debt was paid, which for a poor family meant ruin. Paying to free such men was a recognised charity.
quote: incarcerated for debt

text: The coup d'état of 9 November 1799 (18 Brumaire in the revolutionary calendar) by which Napoleon overthrew the Directory. The Council of the Five Hundred was the lower house that was dispersed at bayonet point. Men who supported the coup were rewarded, this senator among them.
quote: favored the 18 Brumaire

text: Napoleon's Senate was an appointed body of well-paid dignitaries, and a senator might also be given a 'sénatorerie', a country estate with revenues. The office carried prestige and little work, which is why Hugo's senator can be a cheerful epicurean.
quote: a senator of the Empire

text: French for 'welcome'. It was one of the Bishop's baptismal names, and the poor chose it as the one that meant something. Hapgood often translates it, so the same man appears as 'Monseigneur Bienvenu' and 'Monseigneur Welcome'.
quote: Monseigneur Bienvenu

text: A bishop's 'perquisites' were the fees paid for church services beyond the sacraments themselves: publishing marriage banns, granting dispensations (for instance to marry a cousin or in Lent), private baptisms and blessings. The Bishop charged the rich and gave the proceeds away.
quote: the fees for marriage bans, dispensations

text: A small administrative district grouping a handful of villages, the level below the arrondissement and the département. When the Bishop scolds 'the cantons where they were harsh to the poor', he means whole clusters of parishes.
quote: In the cantons where they were harsh

text: Mountain districts of the Hautes-Alpes, the high Alps north of Digne. Briançon is Europe's highest fortified town; Embrun was an ancient archbishopric; the Queyras is a remote valley on the Italian border. The Bishop holds them up as models of neighbourly life.
quote: the valley of Queyras

text: Legal documents had to be written on paper bearing a government stamp, bought at a price: a tax on every lawsuit, contract and petition. Peasants who 'ruined themselves in stamped paper' were litigants paying for endless proceedings.
quote: ruined themselves in stamped paper

text: Itinerant schoolmasters hired themselves out at fairs in the Alps, and advertised their qualifications by the feathers in their hatbands: one for reading, two for reading and arithmetic, three for Latin as well. Hugo took the detail from a real Dauphiné custom.
quote: the quill pens which they wear in the cord of their hat

text: Hapgood's rendering of 'Votre Grandeur', the formal address for a bishop, literally 'Your Greatness'. The Bishop's joke about his greatness not reaching the top shelf depends on that literal sense.
quote: call him Your Grace

text: An entail (substitution) fixed the descent of a title or estate in advance through a line of heirs, so that a nephew could know he would one day be a duke. Madame de Lô's 'expectations' are these future inheritances; the Bishop quietly finds them indecent.
quote: the heir by entail to the title of the Duke

text: Bishop of Hippo (354–430), the most influential of the Latin Church Fathers. The saying the Bishop attributes to him, to put your hopes in the man from whom you will not inherit, is not in Augustine; it is Hugo's own.
quote: to be found, I believe, in St. Augustine

text: Narrow woven braid or ribbon used to trim uniforms, liveries and furniture. M. Géborand made his two millions in coarse cloth and galloon, the unglamorous end of the textile trade.
quote: serges, and woollen galloons

text: The 'Ultras' were the extreme royalist party of the Restoration, more royalist than the king, allied with the Church. A Voltairian was a sceptic who mocked religion in the manner of Voltaire. The two should be opposites, which is Hugo's point about the Marquis de Champtercier.
quote: an ultra-royalist and an ultra-Voltairian

term: the tax on doors and windows
text: A tax introduced in 1798 and assessed on the number of openings in a dwelling, on the theory that more windows meant more wealth. The poor responded by bricking up windows, which is why the Bishop says the law sells air. It lasted until 1926.
quote: the tax on doors and windows

term: Dauphiné, Isère, Var, the two Alpes
text: The mountainous south-east of France. Dauphiné is the old province around Grenoble; the Isère, the Var, the Hautes-Alpes and the Basses-Alpes are the départements carved out of it and Provence after 1790. Digne is the chief town of the Basses-Alpes.
quote: the Alpes, the Hautes, and the Basses

text: Provençal and the related tongues of Languedoc and Dauphiné, varieties of the langue d'oc that most southern peasants spoke instead of French in 1815. The Bishop's scraps of patois mean roughly 'Well, sir, are you wise?', 'Where will you pass?' and 'Bring a good mutton with a good fat cheese'.
quote: the dialect of the south

term: Counterfeiting was still punishable with death
text: Under the Penal Code of 1810, coining false money was a capital crime, as it had been under the old monarchy. The death penalty for it was abolished in 1832, which is why Hugo writes 'still'.
quote: Counterfeiting was still punishable with death

text: The public prosecutor, in French the procureur du roi, or at the Assizes the avocat général. Hapgood translates the office variously as 'attorney for the crown', 'advocate of the crown', 'district-attorney' and 'attorney-general'; they are all the same prosecuting magistrate. The Bishop's question, where will the prosecutor himself be tried, is the first of Hugo's many attacks on judicial zeal.
quote: the attorney for the crown

text: The criminal court that tried serious crimes before a jury, sitting periodically in each département's chief town. Lesser offences went to the 'correctional police' courts without a jury. Hugo's trial scenes all take place at the Assizes.
quote: At the Court of Assizes

text: A fairground performer, juggler or quack who harangued crowds from a platform. The condemned man had also been a 'writer for the public', a scribe who penned letters for the illiterate, so he was half showman, half clerk.
quote: a mountebank at fairs

text: The open cart that carried the condemned to the scaffold, infamous from the Terror. In 1815 the guillotine was still a public spectacle in the town square, which is why the Bishop's presence beside the criminal was so visible.
quote: He mounted the tumbril with him

text: A short cape covering the shoulders, worn by bishops and canons over the cassock; a bishop's is purple. Wearing it with the pectoral cross meant the Bishop went to the scaffold in full episcopal dress.
quote: his purple camail

text: Joseph de Maistre (1753–1821), the Catholic reactionary philosopher, defended the executioner as the cornerstone of society. Cesare Beccaria's 'On Crimes and Punishments' (1764) was the Enlightenment's great argument against torture and the death penalty. Hugo, who campaigned against the guillotine all his life, sets them as the two poles.
quote: like de Maistre; others execrate it, like Beccaria

text: French legal term for the public vengeance exacted by the law (vindicte publique). Hugo uses the word to insist that the guillotine is not neutral machinery but society's act of revenge.
quote: it is called vindicte

text: The smallest everyday coin, one twentieth of a franc, five centimes. People still counted in sous for small sums: a loaf cost a few sous, a labourer earned twenty or thirty a day. M. Géborand's single sou shared among six beggars is Hugo's measure of a miser.
quote: he gave a sou every Sunday

text: A bishop's chief deputies, priests who administered the diocese on his behalf. A canon was a member of the cathedral chapter, a comfortable clerical post. Hugo lists them to show how much routine business a bishop had.
quote: nearly every day his vicars-general

text: The book of daily prayers (the Divine Office) that every priest was bound to recite. 'His offices and his breviary' are the Bishop's fixed devotional duties, before any time for the poor.
quote: his offices and his breviary

text: A monk of the strictest Cistercian observance, founded at La Trappe, vowed to silence and a diet without meat. The town's joke is that the Bishop eats like a Trappist except when a visiting curé gives Madame Magloire an excuse for fish and game.
quote: the cheer of a trappist

text: The author of the Targum, the ancient Aramaic ('Chaldaic') paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible. Flavius Josephus was the first-century Jewish historian. The Bishop comparing their versions of Genesis 1:2 shows him as a scholar as well as a saint.
quote: the Chaldaic paraphrase of Onkelos

term: great-grand-uncle to the writer of this book
text: Hugo is boasting of a (dubious) ancestor, a seventeenth-century bishop of Ptolemaïs named Hugo. The narrator of Les Misérables is openly Victor Hugo himself, who intrudes with family lore, politics and his own travels throughout.
quote: great-grand-uncle to the writer of this book

text: The tenth of produce once owed to the Church, abolished in 1789. The Bishop's joke is that he pays tithes to the hospital, giving half his cows' milk, a reversal of the old flow from poor to clergy.
quote: I am paying my tithes

text: A kneeling desk for prayer: a low step to kneel on with a sloping ledge for a book. The Bishop's are of straw, like all his furniture.
quote: two straw prie-Dieu

text: A deep, wide upholstered armchair of the eighteenth century, 'shepherdess' in French. Mademoiselle Baptistine's gilded bergère, hoisted through a window because the stair was too narrow, is the one relic of comfort in the house.
quote: to hoist this bergère up

text: A stamped mohair velvet, originally from the Dutch town, used for upholstery. A drawing-room set in it with a mahogany sofa was a modest bourgeois dream; Mademoiselle Baptistine saved forty-two francs toward it in five years.
quote: yellow Utrecht velvet

text: The Cistercians, the reformed Benedictine order founded at Cîteaux in Burgundy in 1098. An 'abbé' of Grand-Champ held the revenues of a Cistercian abbey without necessarily living as a monk, a common arrangement before the Revolution.
quote: order of Cîteaux

text: Small discs of dried paste, moistened to seal letters or stick papers together before gummed envelopes existed. The note on the back of the portrait is fixed with four of them.
quote: attached ... with four wafers

text: The great quarrel of eighteenth-century botany. Linnaeus classified plants by counting their sexual parts; Tournefort and then the Jussieu family grouped them by overall 'natural' affinity. The Bishop, says Hugo, took no side: he loved flowers rather than studying plants.
quote: nor with Jussieu against Linnaeus

text: Latin, from Psalm 127 (126 in the Vulgate): 'Unless the Lord keep the house, they watch in vain who guard it.' The Bishop's whole case for an unlocked door is this verse.
quote: Nisi Dominus custodierit domum

text: Dragoons were heavy cavalry, and their colonels a byword for dash and swagger. The Bishop sets the priest's quiet bravery beside the soldier's showy kind.
quote: a colonel of dragoons

text: A real Provençal brigand, Gaspard de Besse (1757–1781), who robbed travellers in the gorges of Ollioules near Toulon and was broken on the wheel at Aix. He became a local Robin Hood figure; Cravatte, his 'lieutenant', is Hugo's invention.
quote: the band of Gaspard Bès

text: The gendarmerie was the military police force that patrolled the countryside and roads, organised in small brigades under a 'brigadier' (a corporal). They checked travellers' papers and hunted brigands. Town police were a separate, civilian body under the prefect.
quote: The gendarmes were set on his track

text: The ancient Latin hymn of thanksgiving, 'We praise thee, O God', sung on great occasions. To 'chant a Te Deum pontifically' is to celebrate it in full bishop's vestments, which the mountain parish does not possess.
quote: to chant a Te Deum pontifically

text: The vestments of a bishop: the cope is the long semicircular cloak worn for ceremonies, the mitre the tall pointed headdress, the crosier the shepherd's-crook staff. A chasuble is the poncho-like garment any priest wears to say mass. Cravatte's chest contains the full pontifical set.
quote: a cope of cloth of gold, a mitre

text: The parish priest's house, the French presbytère; Hapgood also uses 'parsonage' and 'the priest's house'. Visiting bishops lodged there.
quote: deposited in the presbytery

text: Epicurus was the Greek philosopher of tranquil pleasure, a respectable name for a materialist. Pigault-Lebrun (1753–1835) wrote racy, irreligious popular novels. Hugo's jab is that the senator thinks himself a philosopher when he is merely a reader of dirty books.
quote: only a product of Pigault-Lebrun

text: Roman augurs read omens in the flight of birds. Cato is said to have wondered how two augurs could pass each other without laughing, since both knew the business was a fraud. The senator means that he and the Bishop are both in on the trick of religion; the Bishop does not accept the compliment.
quote: We are two augurs

term: the Marquis d’Argens, Pyrrhon, Hobbes, and M. Naigeon
text: The senator's library of unbelievers: d'Argens, a freethinking friend of Frederick the Great; Pyrrho, the Greek sceptic; Hobbes, the English materialist; Naigeon, Diderot's atheist editor. He prefers them to Diderot and Voltaire, whom he finds too religious.
quote: the Marquis d’Argens, Pyrrhon, Hobbes, and M. Naigeon

text: John Needham, an eighteenth-century priest-scientist, claimed to see tiny 'eels' generate spontaneously in flour paste left in vinegar, proof that life needs no creator. Voltaire ridiculed him. The senator takes Needham's side: if paste can make eels, God is superfluous.
quote: Needham’s eels prove that God is useless

text: Latin, 'let there be light', God's first words in Genesis. The senator says a drop of vinegar in paste does the same job.
quote: supplies the fiat lux

text: The Egyptian goddess Isis was said to have an inscription at Sais: 'No mortal has lifted my veil.' To raise it became a figure for penetrating nature's secrets; the senator counts himself among the initiated who have.
quote: raised the veil of Isis

text: Le Moniteur universel, the official government newspaper where laws, appointments and speeches were published. To say something 'in the Moniteur' is to say it publicly and officially; the senator keeps his atheism for private company.
quote: in the Moniteur

text: Sardanapalus, the legendary last king of Assyria, stood for luxury and debauchery; Saint Vincent de Paul (1581–1660) for charity to the poor. The senator's creed is that since death ends everything, it makes no difference which you were.
quote: You have been Sardanapalus, you have been Vincent de Paul

text: A scene from Fénelon's 'Télémaque' (1699), the moral novel about Odysseus's son guided by the goddess Minerva, standard reading for well-brought-up girls. Baptistine muddles it with 'Roman ladies', which tells us how little she minds about such things.
quote: Telemachus being knighted by Minerva

text: The écu, the big silver coin of the old monarchy worth six livres, still in circulation and still used as a unit of reckoning: 'a hundred crowns' meant 300 francs, 'a thousand crowns' 3,000. Regilding two tables for two crowns each was a small luxury the household refused.
quote: two crowns of six francs each

text: Hapgood's literal rendering of 'généralité', a fiscal district of the old monarchy administered by an intendant. Baptistine's genealogy of the Faux family is the kind of pedigree-tracing that still mattered in Restoration drawing-rooms.
quote: the generalship of Caen

text: A member of the highest nobility under the old monarchy, and after 1814 a member of the Chamber of Peers, the upper house of the Restoration parliament, appointed by the king. Peers wore a distinctive costume and sat as a court for political trials.
quote: peer of France

text: The National Convention was the assembly that governed France from September 1792 to 1795: it proclaimed the Republic, tried and condemned Louis XVI, and presided over the Terror. Its surviving members were pariahs under the Restoration, and those who had voted for the king's death ('regicides') were exiled by a law of 1816. G—— voted against the death and so could stay.
quote: a former member of the Convention

text: The Revolution abolished 'Monsieur' in favour of 'citoyen' and encouraged everyone to use the familiar 'tu' as a mark of equality. By 1815 these were damning marks of an old Jacobin.
quote: people called each other “thou,” and when they said “citizen.”

text: The cours prévôtales, special courts set up by the Restoration in 1815 to try political and seditious offences summarily, without appeal, during the 'White Terror' against Bonapartists and revolutionaries. Digne's gossips think G—— should have been hauled before one.
quote: brought before a provost’s court

text: In Islamic tradition, the angel of death who separates the soul from the body. Hugo says even Azrael would have turned back from so vigorous a dying man.
quote: Azrael, the Mohammedan angel of the sepulchre

term: the king who was flesh above and marble below
text: From the Arabian Nights: the young king of the Black Isles, whose sorceress wife turned the lower half of his body to stone while he lived on from the waist up. G——'s legs are dead while his head blazes.
quote: flesh above and marble below

text: The son of Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette, proclaimed king by royalists after his father's execution. He was kept in the Temple prison in Paris, neglected and abused, and died there in 1795 aged ten. For royalists he was the martyred child; G—— sets another child beside him.
quote: Louis XVII?

text: Louis-Dominique Cartouche was the most famous bandit of Paris, broken on the wheel in 1721. His fifteen-year-old brother was sentenced to be hung by the armpits for two hours in the Place de Grève, the public square of executions, and died of it. G——'s point: an innocent child of the people, as pitiable as a royal one.
quote: the brother of Cartouche

text: Latin, 'Suffer the little children' (Mark 10:14), Christ's words when the disciples kept children away. G—— quotes it to say Christ made no distinction between a dauphin and a beggar's child.
quote: ‘Sinite parvulos,’

term: Bossuet chanting the Te Deum over the dragonnades
text: The dragonnades were Louis XIV's method of forcing Protestants to convert: billeting brutal dragoons in their homes. Bossuet, the great court preacher and Bishop of Meaux, celebrated the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685) that followed. G—— answers Marat's guillotine with the monarchy's own atrocities, and wounds the Bishop by touching his hero.
quote: the Te Deum over the dragonnades

text: Men of the Terror: Carrier drowned prisoners in the Loire at Nantes; Fouquier-Tinville was the Revolutionary Tribunal's prosecutor; Maillard led the September Massacres; 'Père Duchesne' was Hébert's foul-mouthed paper; Jourdan 'Head-cutter' massacred at Avignon. G—— pairs each with a persecutor under the kings: Montrevel and Bâville against the Protestants, Saulx-Tavannes at Saint Bartholomew, Letellier and Louvois behind the dragonnades.
quote: Carrier is a bandit; but what name do you give to Montrevel?

text: A French Protestant. After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, Protestant worship was outlawed, ministers banished and those who would not abjure imprisoned, sent to the galleys or tortured; hundreds of thousands fled abroad.
quote: that poor Huguenot woman, who, in 1685

text: Latin, 'I am a worm', from Psalm 22:6. The Bishop's answer when challenged to say who he is; G—— retorts that a worm does not travel by carriage.
quote: Vermis sum—I am a worm

text: The return of the Bourbon monarchy after Napoleon's fall: Louis XVIII, brother of the guillotined Louis XVI, entered Paris in 1814, fled during the Hundred Days, and returned after Waterloo in 1815. The Restoration lasted until 1830. Most of this novel is set in it, and Hugo, writing in 1862, judges it harshly; G—— calls 1814 'that fatal return of the past'.
quote: the past, which is called 1814

text: The bonnet rouge or Phrygian cap, the emblem of the Revolution worn by sans-culottes. The dowager's joke is that the Bishop is turning Jacobin; his reply plays on the red hat of a cardinal, which the same people would revere.
quote: receive the red cap

term: G——, D——, the Marquise de R——
text: Hugo often prints only an initial and a dash for a name or town, in the old novelist's manner of pretending to protect real people. Digne becomes 'D——' in some passages; the conventionist and the charitable marquise are never named. Treat the dashes as part of the book's texture, not as puzzles.
quote: His name was G⸺

text: Napoleon created a new nobility in 1808, with titles of prince, duke, count, baron and knight bestowed for service, and gave many bishops the rank of baron. It sat oddly on a man who gave away his carriage money.
quote: a baron of the Empire

text: Pius VII excommunicated Napoleon in 1809 after the French annexed Rome; on the night of 5–6 July French troops seized him and carried him off to Savona and later Fontainebleau. Napoleon summoned a national council of bishops to Paris in 1811 to get round the Pope's refusal to confirm his bishops. It defied him, and he dissolved it.
quote: The arrest of the Pope took place

text: The two parties in the French Church. Gallicans upheld the traditional independence of the French Church and the king's authority over it; ultramontanes looked 'beyond the mountains' to the Pope's supreme authority. Under Napoleon, gallicanism meant siding with the Emperor against the captive Pope.
quote: an ultramontane rather than a gallican

text: Napoleon's last reign: he escaped from Elba, landed near Cannes on 1 March 1815, marched to Paris as Louis XVIII fled, and ruled until Waterloo in June. Everyone in France had to choose sides, and the Bishop chose the king.
quote: during the Hundred Days

text: Napoleon landed from Elba at Golfe-Juan near Cannes on 1 March 1815 with about a thousand men and marched north through the Alps, by Digne and Grenoble, gathering troops sent to stop him. The Bishop's brother, a general in Provence, pursued him very half-heartedly.
quote: the disembarkation at Cannes

text: The battle of 18 June 1815 near Brussels in which Wellington and Blücher finally defeated Napoleon, ending the Hundred Days and the Empire. Here it is only glimpsed on the horizon of 1815, the year the Bishop's story reaches.
quote: when Waterloo could be dimly discerned

text: The order Napoleon founded in 1802 to reward military and civil merit, its cross worn on a red ribbon. Under the Restoration the Emperor's profile on the medal was replaced by Henri IV's, and the imperial eagle by Bourbon fleurs-de-lys, which the old soldier calls 'three frogs'. A 'chevalier' is the lowest grade.
quote: a member of the Legion of Honor at Austerlitz

text: A supporter of Napoleon and his dynasty after 1815. Bonapartists were watched by the Restoration police, prosecuted for 'seditious speeches' and dismissed from posts; the cult of the exiled Emperor among old soldiers and the common people runs through the novel.
quote: as much of a Bonapartist as the eagle

text: The Bourbon king restored in 1814, younger brother of Louis XVI. He was elderly, enormously fat and crippled with gout, had spent his exile partly in England (hence the 'English gaiters'), and wore the old-fashioned powdered queue or pigtail. Bonapartists despised him; he reigned until 1824.
quote: to scoff aloud at Louis XVIII

text: A lay church officer who kept order during services and led processions, usually a dignified ex-soldier in a braided coat with a staff. The Bishop finds the dismissed Bonapartist porter this harmless post.
quote: appointed him beadle in the cathedral

text: Originally an abbot, but by the eighteenth century a courtesy title for any young secular priest or cleric. 'Little abbés' are the ambitious junior clergy who attach themselves to a rising bishop; the Bishop of Digne has none.
quote: a full squadron of little abbés

text: Francis de Sales (1567–1622), Bishop of Geneva and author of the 'Introduction to the Devout Life', famous for gentleness and wit. 'Prêtres blancs-becs', callow priests, literally 'white-beaks', is his phrase for fledgling clergy.
quote: that charming Saint François de Sales

text: The paid positions of the Church: a prebend was the income attached to a cathedral stall, an archdeacon a bishop's regional deputy, a canon a member of the chapter. These were the 'nice little promotions' a well-connected bishop could scatter among favourites.
quote: prebends, archidiaconates, chaplaincies

term: from a Grace to an Eminence
text: The ladder of Roman ecclesiastical titles. A bishop is 'Your Grace' (Grandeur), a cardinal 'Your Eminence', the Pope 'Your Holiness'. The pallium is the woollen band the Pope gives archbishops; a conclavist is a cardinal's attendant at a papal election; an auditor and a papal chamberlain are posts at the Roman court.
quote: from a Grace to an Eminence is only a step

text: From La Fontaine's fable 'The Milkmaid and the Pot of Milk': Perrette carries milk to market dreaming of the eggs, chickens, pig and cow it will buy, skips, and spills it all. Any daydream of future riches is 'Perrette's pot'.
quote: Perrette’s pot of milk

text: The identical twins of Plautus's comedy 'Menaechmi', the source of Shakespeare's 'Comedy of Errors'. Success is talent's twin, Hugo says: so alike that history mistakes one for the other.
quote: that Menaechmus of talent

text: The Roman satirist and the Roman historian, both merciless about the corruption and sycophancy of imperial Rome. Hugo claims them as the only writers who refuse to flatter success.
quote: Juvenal and Tacitus alone grumble at it

text: One of the Republic's armies of the 1790s, fighting on the Belgian and Rhine frontier. Hugo's apothecary who got rich selling cardboard boot-soles to it stands for every war profiteer; the contractors who starved the revolutionary armies were a national scandal.
quote: the army of the Sambre-and-Meuse

text: Latin, 'I believe in the Father', the opening of the Creed. Hugo offers it as the sum of what can be known of the Bishop's orthodoxy.
quote: “Credo in Patrem,” he often exclaimed

text: Latin, 'because she loved much', Christ's words forgiving the sinful woman in Luke 7:47. Hugo applies it to the Bishop: his 'excess of love' is what 'serious men' hold against him.
quote: quia multum amavit

term: “Who knoweth whither the soul of the animal goeth?”
text: Ecclesiastes 3:21, which doubts whether a beast's spirit goes down to the earth and man's upward. Hugo cites it for the Bishop's tenderness to spiders and ants, a sentiment he says is rare in priests.
quote: Who knoweth whither the soul of the animal goeth?

text: Pope from 1831 to 1846, a rigid reactionary who condemned liberalism and railways alike. Hugo's aside that he 'held himself erect' but was 'a bad bishop' is the exiled republican of 1862 settling a score.
quote: Gregory XVI, at the age of eighty

text: Pantheism identifies God with nature as a whole, a charge Catholic critics flung at Romantic writers, Hugo among them. He heads it off: the Bishop's night meditations under the stars are not a philosophy but a heart.
quote: a certain “pantheistical” physiognomy

text: Emanuel Swedenborg, the Swedish scientist turned visionary who described conversations with angels; Blaise Pascal, the mathematician whose religious terror of the infinite spaces haunted his later years. Hugo names them as great minds whom contemplation of the absolute drove toward madness.
quote: like Swedenborg and Pascal

text: The prophet Elijah's cloak, with which he parted the Jordan and which fell to Elisha when he was taken up to heaven (2 Kings 2). A chasuble with its folds would be a prophet's garment; the Bishop, Hugo says, had nothing of the prophet.
quote: the folds of Elijah’s mantle

text: Four minds who stared into the abyss of being: the Roman poet of atoms and death, Manu the legendary Hindu lawgiver, the apostle, and the poet of Hell. Hugo sets them as the 'archangels of the human mind' whose questions the Bishop declined to ask.
quote: Lucretius, Manou, Saint Paul, Dante

text: Digne's tree-lined promenade, named for the philosopher Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a native of the district who was Descartes's great opponent. Hugo visited Digne and uses its real streets, fountains and inns.
quote: the boulevard Gassendi

term: the proclamation of the Gulf Juan
text: The manifesto Napoleon issued on landing from Elba on 1 March 1815, promising to reclaim his throne. General Drouot read it to the people of Digne on 4 March as the Emperor passed through; a Digne printer first printed the proclamations dictated on Elba. Jean Valjean enters the town by the same street seven months later.
quote: the proclamation of the Gulf Juan

text: The Grenoble inn where Napoleon lodged on 7 March 1815 rather than at the prefecture, saying he was going to a brave man's house. The Guides were his personal escort cavalry; General Bertrand, his Grand Marshal, followed him to Elba and Saint Helena. The Digne innkeeper Labarre borrows glory from his Grenoble cousin.
quote: the inn of the Three Dauphins in Grenoble

text: The French league (lieue) was about four kilometres, two and a half miles. Twelve leagues is nearly fifty kilometres, a brutal day's walk.
quote: I have travelled twelve leagues

text: Provençal patois, roughly 'it's the prowler' (ço es lo maraud): the word that has gone round Digne for the stranger. It shows how fast the innkeeper's note to the town hall has travelled.
quote: “Tso-maraude.”

text: 'The covered rose', a term from French stick-fencing (bâton): a whirling guard that keeps the staff moving around the body. Jean Valjean knows it, and uses it to back out of a dog's kennel.
quote: la rose couverte

text: The civil wars between Catholics and Protestants that tore France apart from 1562 to 1598. Digne, in a region with many Protestants, was besieged more than once, and in 1815 still had its sixteenth-century walls and towers.
quote: sieges during the wars of religion

text: A small gold cross hung on a black velvet ribbon round the neck, the traditional ornament of French peasant and servant women. It is Madame Magloire's one piece of jewellery.
quote: a gold Jeannette cross on a velvet ribbon

text: A fichu is a triangular kerchief worn over the shoulders and tucked into the bodice; a stomacher is the decorative panel covering the front of the bodice. Madame Magloire dresses like a Marseilles working woman; Mademoiselle Baptistine like a lady of 1806, in a high-waisted Empire gown worn for ten years.
quote: a very white fichu

text: A small frizzed wig (perruque à l'enfant) worn by elderly ladies to cover grey hair, a fashion of the late eighteenth century. Baptistine's wig and 1806 gown mark her as gently out of date.
quote: known as the “baby wig.”

text: A gypsy, and by extension any rootless vagrant. Madame Magloire's gossip turns a tired traveller into 'a Bohemian, a barefooted vagabond', the standard picture of a dangerous outsider.
quote: a Bohemian, a barefooted vagabond

text: The bagne, the prison for men sentenced to hard labour. The name survived from the oared galleys of Louis XIV, long gone; by 1815 'galley-slaves' worked in chains in the naval dockyards of Toulon, Brest and Rochefort. Sentences were counted in years of the galleys or 'for life', and the word carried a lifelong stain.
quote: a convict from the galleys

text: A liberated convict received a passport printed on yellow paper, recording his crime and sentence and marking him as under police surveillance. He had to show it in every town and follow a prescribed route to an assigned residence. It made honest work and lodging almost impossible, which is Hugo's point.
quote: my yellow passport

text: A town in the Jura mountains near the Swiss border, in Franche-Comté. It is the place of residence assigned to Jean Valjean on his passport, the far end of a forced march across France.
quote: on my way to Pontarlier

text: Hapgood's rendering of 'la Major', the old cathedral of Marseilles. Bishops sometimes said mass for the convicts in the Toulon yard, with the men ranged in lines under loaded cannon: Jean Valjean's only idea of what a bishop is.
quote: the Bishop of Majore at Marseilles

term: the red coat, the ball on the ankle
text: Convict dress and irons: a red woollen jacket or smock, a numbered cap, and a chain riveted to an iron ring on the ankle, often ending in a cannonball or linking two men together. The 'double chain' was a punishment, the 'cell' solitary confinement. Jean Valjean's catalogue is the galleys in a sentence.
quote: the red coat, the ball on the ankle

text: The frigate Méduse ran aground off Africa in July 1816; 150 people were set adrift on a raft and only fifteen survived after thirteen days of thirst, murder and cannibalism. Géricault's huge painting made it the scandal of the Restoration. 'A glass of water to one of the shipwrecked' is Hugo's image of what 'Monsieur' means to a convict.
quote: the shipwrecked of the Medusa

text: Wine from Mauves on the Rhône, in the Saint-Joseph vineyards, a good local red. The Bishop keeps a bottle for guests and never drinks it himself, because wine is dear.
quote: his old Mauves wine

text: French distinguishes the familiar 'tu' from the respectful 'vous'. Convicts, servants and beggars were addressed as 'tu' by their superiors as a matter of course, so when the Bishop says 'Monsieur' and 'vous' to Jean Valjean it is almost unbearable to him. Hapgood marks the contemptuous form with 'thou'.
quote: You do not address me as thou?

text: The Bishop paraphrases Luke 15:7, from the parable of the lost sheep: more rejoicing over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine just men. It is the only sermon he allows himself.
quote: There will be more joy in heaven

text: The old province on the Swiss border around Besançon and Pontarlier, mountainous, forested, with iron foundries, watchmaking and dairies. The Bishop took refuge there during the Revolution and worked with his hands, which is why he can describe its industries to a man who needs a trade.
quote: I took refuge in Franche-Comté

text: The cooperative cheese-dairies of the Jura, where peasants pooled their cows' milk to make the great wheels of Comté (Gruyère) cheese. The grurin is the hired cheesemaker who records each member's milk on a tally stick. The Bishop dwells on the trade as a quiet hint of an honest living.
quote: which they call fruitières

text: The ancien régime: France before 1789, with its king, nobility, provinces and venal offices. A 'captain of the gates' was one of its small military sinecures. Baptistine's relative held one; the Revolution swept such things away along with the family's fortune.
quote: captain of the gates at Pontarlier under the old regime

term: snuffing out his candle with his nostrils
text: Convicts had no snuffers and learned to put out a candle by blowing sharply down through the nose. Hugo gives the detail as a reflex the galleys have left in Jean Valjean's body, along with sleeping in his clothes.
quote: Snuffing out his candle with his nostrils after the manner of convicts

text: Brie is the flat farming country east of Paris, known for its cheese. Faverolles, in the Aisne on its edge, is the village where Jean Valjean was a tree-pruner (élagueur), a seasonal labourer who trimmed orchards and roadside trees.
quote: a tree-pruner at Faverolles

text: Puerperal fever, the often fatal infection that killed many women after childbirth, blamed at the time on the onset of the milk. Jean Valjean's mother died of it for want of care.
quote: died of a milk fever

text: A pruner's wage, less than a franc, in a season when the work existed at all. A four-pound loaf cost around twelve to fifteen sous in a bad year, so feeding eight people on this was impossible, which is the arithmetic behind the theft.
quote: he earned eighteen sous a day

text: The Penal Code of 1791 punished theft committed at night, by breaking into an inhabited house, with years in irons regardless of the value stolen. Hugo's charge is that the law was 'explicit' and therefore blind: a loaf and a broken pane carried five years.
quote: The terms of the Code were explicit

text: The revolutionary calendar renamed the months and counted years from the Republic's founding in 1792; 2 Floréal, year IV is 21 April 1796. 'Buona-Parte' is the Italian spelling of the young general's name, which the Directory's message still used. Hugo sets Napoleon's first victory at Montenotte against Jean Valjean's chaining on the same day.
quote: the 2nd of Floréal, year IV

text: A vast old hospital-prison south of Paris where convicts from all over northern France were gathered twice a year into the 'chain', riveted together by the neck in the courtyard, then marched or carted to the galleys. Jean Valjean's twenty-seven-day journey to Toulon began there.
quote: put in chains at Bicêtre

text: Each convict was known by his register number and nothing else. Jean Valjean's number at Toulon is 24,601. The number is Hugo's way of saying the man himself has been erased.
quote: he was number 24,601

text: Because the galleys belonged to the Navy, offences inside them, escapes above all, were judged by a special naval court that could add years to a sentence without a jury. Four escape attempts turned Jean Valjean's five years into nineteen.
quote: The maritime tribunal condemned him

text: Hugo means Claude Gueux, the hero of his own 1834 story of that name: a real Troyes workman who stole bread to feed his family, killed a prison warder and was guillotined. Hugo cites his earlier book as evidence that hunger is where the law's disasters begin.
quote: Claude Gaux had stolen a loaf

text: The Brothers of the Christian Schools, the teaching order founded by Jean-Baptiste de La Salle, nicknamed 'Ignorantins' because they taught the poor and took no holy orders. They ran the school in the Toulon galleys where Jean Valjean learned to read at forty.
quote: kept by the Ignorantin friars

term: Dante at the portals of hell
text: The inscription over the gate of Hell in Dante's Inferno ends 'Abandon all hope, you who enter.' Hugo's physiologist would do the same to Jean Valjean's soul: erase the word hope.
quote: like Dante at the portals of hell

text: A jackscrew (cric) is the screw-jack used to lift carts and heavy loads. Hugo adds that the old French word for it was 'orgueil', pride, whence the Rue Montorgueil in Paris. Jean Valjean's nickname in the galleys is for a man who can lift what a machine lifts.
quote: nicknamed him Jean the Jackscrew

text: Pierre Puget (1620–1694), the great Baroque sculptor of Provence, carved the two straining stone atlantes that hold up the balcony of Toulon's town hall, a landmark of the port. Jean Valjean is said to have shouldered one when it came loose.
quote: those admirable caryatids of Puget

text: The garde-chiourme, the warder of a gang of convicts, armed with a cudgel and a whip. In Jean Valjean's vision of society he is the nearest tier of the pyramid that crushes him, with the gendarme and the archbishop above and the Emperor at the top.
quote: the galley-sergeant and his cudgel

text: The perfume town in the hills above Cannes, surrounded by fields of orange trees, roses and jasmine distilled for scent. Jean Valjean's first day's work as a free man, unloading bales at an orange-flower distillery, earns him half the agreed wage.
quote: an orange-flower distillery

text: A heavy iron spike with a socket for a candle, driven into rock to light a quarry face. Convicts quarried stone in the hills round Toulon and could get hold of such tools. In the dark it is simply a short pointed iron bar.
quote: a miner’s candlestick

text: Lot's wife, turned to a pillar of salt when she looked back at Sodom (Genesis 19:26). Jean Valjean freezes like her at the shriek of the Bishop's door hinge.
quote: petrified like the statue of salt

text: The ring a bishop wears as a sign of his office, kissed by the faithful. It is on the hand that hangs over the edge of the bed as the Bishop sleeps.
quote: adorned with the pastoral ring

text: The non-commissioned officer commanding a small gendarmerie post, equivalent to a corporal, not a general as in English. He salutes the Bishop as a superior and takes his word without question.
quote: A brigadier of gendarmes

text: Boys from the poor Alpine duchy of Savoy, then outside France, came down each winter to earn pennies as chimney-sweeps, street musicians and showmen, with a hurdy-gurdy and a trained marmot in a box. They were the type of the homeless child, and Hugo's Little Gervais is one.
quote: a little Savoyard

text: A silver two-franc coin, which the child calls his 'white piece'. It is a day's wages for a labourer and the boy's whole fortune.
quote: one forty-sou piece

text: The big silver coin of the period, also called an écu or 'a hundred sous'; working people nicknamed it a 'hind wheel' for its size. Jean Valjean presses two, then two more, on the priest, a sum a peasant family might live on for a fortnight.
quote: two five-franc pieces

text: Louis XVIII dated his reign from 1795, when the boy Louis XVII died in prison, as if the Republic and the Empire had never happened. So 1817 was officially his twenty-second year, though he had sat on the throne for barely three. Hugo opens the Book with this royal fiction.
quote: entitled the twenty-second of his reign

text: The stylised lily, emblem of the French kings. After 1814 it replaced the imperial eagle and bees everywhere, on coins, shop signs and buttonholes, and loyal citizens wore a silver lily on a white ribbon. Scratching off Napoleon's N's from the Louvre was the same campaign in reverse.
quote: decked with fleurs-de-lys

text: The remote British island in the South Atlantic where Napoleon was sent after Waterloo and kept under guard. He was there from October 1815 until his death in 1821. Hugo's detail that he had his old coats turned, for want of green cloth, is a jab at his English jailers.
quote: Napoleon was at St. Helena

text: The grand ceremony Napoleon staged on the Champ de Mars in Paris on 1 June 1815, during the Hundred Days, to swear in a new constitution before the army. Hugo enjoys the absurdity: the 'Field of May' was held in June on the 'Field of March'. Two years later its painted columns lie rotting in the grass.
quote: the Emperor’s platform in the Champ de Mai

text: Talleyrand, a bishop under the old monarchy, served the Revolution, Napoleon and then the Bourbons in turn; the Abbé Louis was the Restoration's finance minister. Both had officiated at the patriotic mass of the Festival of Federation on 14 July 1790. Hugo reuses the 'two augurs' who cannot look at each other without laughing.
quote: laughed as they looked at each other, with the laugh of the two augurs

text: The constitution Louis XVIII 'granted' in 1814: a king with real power, two chambers elected by a tiny wealthy electorate, and guarantees of some revolutionary gains. It was the Restoration's compromise between the old monarchy and the Revolution, so 'the snuffbox à la Charter' and the king's title 'Immortal Author of the Charter' were political fashions.
quote: the snuffbox à la Charter

text: The Duc de Berry, the king's nephew, was the Bourbons' hope for an heir. In February 1820 a saddler named Louvel stabbed him to death outside the Opéra, to end the dynasty. In 1817 Hugo can show him newly married and 'surveyed from the shadow' by his future killer.
quote: already surveyed from the shadow by Louvel

text: Two cafés in the Palais-Royal that served as political clubs: Lemblin was the haunt of Bonapartist half-pay officers, the Valois of old royalists. Under the Restoration even where one drank one's coffee declared one's side.
quote: The Café Lemblin stood up for the Emperor

text: The members of the Convention who had voted for the death of Louis XVI in 1793. In 1816 those who had rallied to Napoleon in the Hundred Days were banished from France. Whether one said 'the regicides' or 'the voters', 'Napoleon' or 'Bonaparte', 'the allies' or 'the enemies', placed one instantly.
quote: the regicides, or to say the voters

text: François-René de Chateaubriand (1768–1848), the great Romantic writer and royalist statesman, the literary idol of Hugo's youth. 'The Monarchy According to the Charter' (1816) was his political pamphlet. Hugo's picture of him cleaning his teeth while dictating is affectionate mockery.
quote: Chateaubriand stood every morning at his window

text: Used alone and capitalised, 'Monsieur' was the title of the king's eldest brother: here the Comte d'Artois, leader of the Ultras. 'Madame' likewise meant the senior royal lady, the Duchesse d'Angoulême, daughter of Louis XVI. The Duc d'Angoulême was the heir's elder cousin, the Duc d'Orléans the head of a rival branch.
quote: with Monsieur’s approval

text: Napoleon's only legitimate son (1811–1832), given the title at birth. After 1815 he lived in Vienna with his mother's Austrian family. For Bonapartists he was 'Napoleon II'; schoolboys wearing the Bourbon lily fought over him.
quote: apropos of the King of Rome

text: Steam navigation was being tried on the Seine in the late 1810s, and Parisians treated it as a toy. Hugo, writing in 1862 when steam had transformed travel, savours the shortsightedness. He uses the same device for the obscure Fourier, the socialist thinker, overshadowed by the famous mathematician of the same name.
quote: an utopia—a steamboat

text: The Hôtel des Invalides, Louis XIV's great home for old and wounded soldiers, with its gilded dome, where Napoleon's veterans lived out their days. Its pensioners were issued large blue cotton handkerchiefs, a familiar sight in Paris.
quote: having the dome of the Invalides regilded

text: Provincial young men of good family went to Paris to study law or medicine, lived in the Latin Quarter on allowances from home, and often took years over their degrees. Tholomyès, an 'antique old student' of thirty with four thousand francs a year, is the type at its most comfortable.
quote: when one says student, one says Parisian

text: Ossian, the Scottish bard of James Macpherson's forged 'ancient' poems (1760s), was a European craze, and Napoleon loved him. Fashionable parents named their sons Oscar after Ossian's son. Hugo's joke is that the four students belong to a generation of Oscars, before Wellington made 'Arthur' the smart name.
quote: They were four Oscars

text: Young working women of Paris, seamstresses, milliners and shop girls, named for the cheap grey cloth they wore. The grisette who lived with a student for a few years, without marriage, was a stock figure of Parisian life and literature, treated lightly by everyone except Hugo.
quote: throngs of students and grisettes

text: The hill on the left bank crowned by the Panthéon, heart of the Latin Quarter, where the schools and colleges of the University stood. To have four thousand francs a year there was riches beside the usual student's pinched allowance.
quote: a splendid scandal on Mount Sainte-Geneviève

text: The Théâtre du Vaudeville in Paris specialised in light comedies with songs. Having a piece rejected there marks Tholomyès as a dabbler in wit, not a writer.
quote: He had had a piece rejected at the Vaudeville

text: Hugo writes from 1862, looking back to 1817, and often reminds the reader of the gap: the railway and the steamboat have since replaced the coach and the rowing-boat, and Paris has swallowed its villages. The past in this book is always seen from the narrator's present.
quote: forty-five years ago

text: A royal château and park on the Seine west of Paris, open to the public, with famous cascades and fountains. It was the classic Sunday outing for Parisians of modest means, reached by coach or by boat.
quote: they went to Saint-Cloud by the coach

text: A light muslin bodice or sleeveless jacket worn over a gown, fashionable in the 1810s. Hugo's derivation from 'quinze août' (15 August) spoken in a Marseilles accent is a playful folk etymology. With her mauve barège gown, a light gauzy wool, it is Fantine's whole summer finery.
quote: whose name, canezou, a corruption of the words quinze août

text: A sturdy yellowish cotton cloth, originally from Nanjing, used for summer trousers. Tholomyès's wide 'elephant-leg' nankeen trousers and his cigar, still a novelty, are the dandy's uniform of 1817.
quote: elephant-leg pattern of nankeen

text: Watteau's painting 'Pilgrimage to Cythera' (1717) shows elegant couples on the island of Venus, the classic image of a lovers' outing. Hugo calls on Watteau, Lancret, Diderot and d'Urfé, author of the pastoral romance 'L'Astrée', as connoisseurs of such idylls.
quote: The departure for Cythera! exclaims Watteau

text: The 'montagnes russes', an early roller coaster: cars running on rails down an undulating wooden track, imported from the ice slides of Russia. The one in the Beaujon gardens near the Champs-Élysées was a sensation of 1817.
quote: sliding down the Russian mountains

text: Paris was ringed by the customs wall of the Farmers-General, with gates called barriers where duty (the octroi) was paid on goods entering the city. The Étoile barrier stood at the top of the Champs-Élysées, where the Arc de Triomphe was then unfinished.
quote: they reached the barrier of l’Étoile

text: The plain white banner of the Bourbon monarchy, restored in 1814 in place of the revolutionary tricolour. To fly it over the Tuileries palace was to say that the Revolution was over; Bonapartists kept the tricolour as a forbidden emblem.
quote: the white flag, showing faintly rosy

text: 'Give us back our father from Ghent': a royalist song of 1815, when Louis XVIII had fled to Ghent during the Hundred Days. Opponents turned it into a pun on 'gant' (glove) to mock a king who returned behind foreign armies.
quote: Rendez-nous notre père de Gand

text: The great square at the foot of the Champs-Élysées, renamed Place de la Révolution in 1792, when the guillotine stood there and Louis XVI was beheaded. It became Place de la Concorde in 1795 and was given back its royal name at the Restoration, until 1830.
quote: which had become the Place Louis XV once more

text: Count Jules Anglès, prefect of police of Paris from 1815 to 1821. His reassuring report on the 'amiable rabble' of the suburbs gives Hugo the cue for a warning about what the Paris populace can do.
quote: Chief of Police Anglès

text: On 10 August 1792 the armed people of the Paris faubourgs stormed the Tuileries palace and overthrew the monarchy. Hugo pairs it with Austerlitz, Napoleon's greatest victory, as proof that the 'little man of the faubourgs' becomes a giant when roused.
quote: he will produce the 10th of August

text: Two songs of the Revolution. 'La Carmagnole' was a jeering dance-song against the king and queen; the 'Marseillaise', written in 1792 and sung by volunteers from Marseilles, became the anthem of the Republic and was banned under the Restoration. Hugo's point: one topples a king, the other frees the world.
quote: nothing but “la Carmagnole,”

text: The mountain pass where the Samnites trapped a Roman army in 321 BC and forced it to march out under a yoke of spears in humiliation. Hugo says the Paris workman will make any narrow street a trap of the same kind.
quote: Caudine Forks

text: Guillaume Coustou's two great marble groups of rearing horses held by grooms, carved for the royal château of Marly and set at the entrance of the Champs-Élysées in 1795. They were a Paris landmark.
quote: The horses of Marly

text: Melancholy or low spirits, thought to come from the spleen; the French borrowed the English word in the eighteenth century, and to 'have the spleen' was fashionably English. Favorite's version is a grisette's grumble about rain, stingy lovers and the price of butter.
quote: I have the spleen, as the English say

text: The church officer who leads the singing in a parish, a modest lay or clerical post. Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas is a Latin Quarter church; Favorite's young actor is a precentor's son who copies documents for an attorney at twenty sous a day.
quote: a former precentor of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas

text: Latin, 'there is a measure in things', from Horace's Satires. Tholomyès stuffs his mock sermon on moderation with Latin tags, puns and pedantry, the showing-off of a law student who has stayed too long at school.
quote: Est modus in rebus

text: The formal name of the citizens of ancient Rome, used in solemn address. Tholomyès mixes it with 'caballeros' and 'gentlemen' in a parody of oratory; his 'Sylla' is Sulla, the Roman dictator who unexpectedly laid down his power.
quote: Quirites, gentlemen, caballeros, my friends

text: Alexandre Grimod de la Reynière (1758–1837), the first great French food writer, author of the 'Almanach des Gourmands'. Tholomyès claims him and Talleyrand, a famous host, as authorities for eating slowly.
quote: Grimod de la Reynière agrees with Talleyrand

text: 'By God', a mild French oath. Hapgood leaves many such exclamations in French (Pardieu, Mon Dieu, Parbleu); they are everyday expletives, not blasphemies.
quote: “Pardieu,” said Tholomyès.

text: Jean Elleviou (1769–1842), the celebrated tenor of the Opéra-Comique. To call the nightingale 'a gratuitous Elleviou' is to say it gives a star's performance for free.
quote: a gratuitous Elleviou

text: The two great rationalist philosophers of the seventeenth century, a serious student's question. Tholomyès answers 'Désaugiers', a writer of drinking songs, and then turns 'Berquin', a children's author, into the pun 'Ber-Choux'. Every reply is a dodge.
quote: Which do you prefer, Descartes or Spinoza?

text: Latin, 'nothing new under the sun', from Ecclesiastes 1:9; 'amor omnibus idem', 'love is the same for all', is from Virgil's Georgics. Tholomyès's punning 'Carabine' and 'Carabin' is student slang for a grisette and a medical student.
quote: Nil sub sole novum

text: The brilliant mistress of Pericles in fifth-century Athens, admired by Socrates. Tholomyès calls her 'Socrates plus Manon Lescaut', joining the philosopher to the heroine of Prévost's novel of a fatally charming kept woman.
quote: Do you know what Aspasia was, ladies?

text: A carter's oath, here glossed as 'the jade'. Tholomyès makes a pun on Malherbe's famous elegy, in which a girl lived 'the space of a morning' (matin); his horse lived 'the space of a mâtin'. It is a callous joke over a dying animal.
quote: the sacramental word, Mâtin

text: The big public stagecoaches that carried passengers and mail between towns, with several compartments and luggage piled on the roof under a tarpaulin. They travelled day and night and kept to timetables, stopping only at fixed posts, which is why Fantine is surprised to see one halt.
quote: the departure of the mail-coaches and diligences

text: Laffitte, Caillard et Compagnie ran the great coaching service of the day, rivals of the Messageries royales. The students' joke is that they flee 'in the arms of Laffitte and on the wings of Caillard', that is, by stagecoach, at three leagues an hour.
quote: in the arms of Laffitte and on the wings of Caillard

text: The parable in Luke 15 of the son who wastes his inheritance and is welcomed home with a fatted calf. The students' letter turns it inside out: they go back to their families, and to careers as prefects and magistrates, as if returning were a sacrifice.
quote: call us prodigal sons

text: A village on a wooded plateau about fifteen kilometres east of Paris, beyond Livry and Chelles, in the forest of Bondy. In 1818 it was quiet countryside, a day's walk from the city, reached by the little suburban coaches.
quote: There was, at Montfermeil, near Paris

text: Inns were known by their painted signboards. This one shows a soldier carrying a wounded general off a smoky battlefield, a scene of heroism at Waterloo, the battle of 1815 that ended Napoleon's reign. Its spelling 'Sargent' is part of the sign's roughness.
quote: At the sign of Sergeant of Waterloo

text: A fine, costly bobbin lace from Valenciennes in northern France. Fantine has dressed her child in it while she herself wears coarse linen, the one vanity she has kept.
quote: Valenciennes lace on her cap

text: It was common, among workers and the middle class alike, to send a baby or small child to be boarded by a woman in the country for a monthly fee. A working mother with no husband had little choice. Seven francs a month, with six months in advance, is a steep but plausible rate.
quote: I will give you six francs a month

text: Louis-Philippe, Duc d'Orléans, of the younger branch of the royal family, became King of the French after the revolution of July 1830 and reigned until 1848. Hugo uses his reign as a later fixed point when he dismisses Tholomyès from the story.
quote: under King Louis Philippe

text: An unpaid promissory note was formally 'protested' by a bailiff (huissier), the first step to seizure of goods and prison for debt. Thénardier's note for 110 francs falls due the next day, which is why the stranger's 57 francs come so pat.
quote: I should have had a bailiff and a protest after me

text: Clélie was Mademoiselle de Scudéry's vast heroic romance of the 1650s; Lodoïska a sentimental tale of the 1790s. Hugo traces the long slide of the romance from the salons to the porters' lodges, down to the cheap novels Madame Thénardier devours.
quote: after having been Clélie, was no longer anything but Lodoïska

text: Epponina was a Gaulish heroine of the first century who hid her rebel husband for nine years and died with him under Vespasian, a favourite of romances. Gulnare is the heroine of Byron's 'The Corsair'; Ducray-Duminil wrote popular novels. The Thénardier girls are named out of their mother's reading.
quote: her eldest daughter was named Éponine

text: Megaera is one of the Furies of Greek myth, a byword for a shrew; Pamela the virtuous servant-girl heroine of Richardson's novel. Hugo sums up Madame Thénardier's whole development in the passage from one to the other.
quote: when the Megaera began to be developed from the Pamela

text: The Mont-de-Piété, the state pawnshop of Paris, lent money against goods at interest. Pawning was a routine part of poor people's budgets. Madame Thénardier gets sixty francs for the outfit Fantine was so proud of.
quote: pawned it at the pawnbroker’s for sixty francs

text: Martin Dumollard, a murderer of servant girls near Lyons, tried and guillotined in 1862 as Hugo was finishing the novel. Hugo cites the court record that he had been 'working for his living' alone since the age of five.
quote: a man named Dumollard

text: A small walled hill town in the Pas-de-Calais, in northern France near the Channel coast, with an upper and a lower town; despite its name it is some way inland. Hapgood often abbreviates it, as Hugo does, to M. sur M.
quote: had reached Montreuil-sur-Mer

term: English jet and black glass trinkets
text: Jet is a black fossil stone, polished for mourning jewellery and beads; it came chiefly from Whitby in England. Cheap imitations were made of black glass. Replacing costly resin with gum-lac (shellac) is the kind of small technical trick that made a provincial fortune in the early industrial age.
quote: the imitation of English jet and the black glass trinkets of Germany

text: 'Father' (le père) before a surname was the familiar way of naming a working man or an older man of the people, like 'old so-and-so' in English. The narrator tracks the stranger's rise through his names: Father Madeleine, then Monsieur Madeleine, then Monsieur le Maire.
quote: He was called Father Madeleine

text: Jacques Laffitte (1767–1844), the most famous Paris banker of the Restoration, governor of the Bank of France and a leading liberal. Having money 'with Laffitte' was the period's shorthand for a fortune safely banked in Paris.
quote: lodged in his name with Laffitte

text: Under the Restoration mayors were not elected: the king appointed them, on the prefect's recommendation, and the appointment appeared in the Moniteur. The mayor was head of the town's administration and its municipal police. Refusing the office, as Father Madeleine first does, was a rare snub to royal favour.
quote: to be appointed by the King, mayor of Montreuil-sur-Mer

text: A short, spoken mass said early in the morning without music, attended by servants and working people. High mass, with singing and full ceremony, and vespers in the afternoon were the services where the respectable were seen. The deputy's piety is for show.
quote: He went regularly to low mass every Sunday

text: Joseph Fouché (1759–1820), once a teacher in the Oratorian order, then a regicide of the Convention and Napoleon's dreaded minister of police; he served Louis XVIII briefly in 1815. Hugo's irony is that the deputy shares 'the religious ideas' of this famous unbeliever.
quote: Fouché, Duc d’Otrante

text: The salle d'asile, a day nursery and school for the small children of working mothers, was just being imported from England in the 1820s; the first in Paris opened in 1826. Madeleine's is ahead of its time, like his dispensary and workers' fund.
quote: an infant school, a thing then almost unknown in France

text: Hapgood's spelling of 'orvale', clary sage, a strong-smelling herb hung up to drive off weevils. Madeleine's farming 'recipes', from salted water for wheat blight to nettles as fodder and cloth, mark him as someone who knows country work at first hand.
quote: hanging up orviot in bloom everywhere

text: Silver plate was stamped by the state assay office to guarantee its purity, so a hallmark proved that an object was real silver and not plated. The ladies of the town take their wit from noticing it.
quote: “for they were hall-marked,”

text: An old phrase for dying with a reputation for holiness, from the belief that saints' bodies gave off a sweet scent. It is the language of the newspaper notice, not a formal title.
quote: died in the odor of sanctity

text: Mourning was strictly codified: black clothes, and a band of black crape round the hat for a man, worn for a set period according to how close the dead person had been. Public mourning for someone was a claim of connection, which is why the town gossips read it as one.
quote: with crape on his hat

text: The aristocratic quarter of the Left Bank in Paris, home of the old nobility after the Restoration and a byword for exclusive royalist society. Every provincial town had its 'microscopic Faubourg Saint-Germain' of local gentry.
quote: The microscopic Faubourg Saint-Germain

text: An inspector of police was a mid-ranking officer who carried out the investigations and arrests; in a small town he was the police. Javert owes his post to the patronage of the prefect of police in Paris, Comte Anglès.
quote: the unpleasant but useful functions of an inspector

text: A released convict was placed under surveillance and forbidden to live outside his assigned place; to 'break one's ban' (rompre son ban) was to leave it, a crime that sent a man back to the galleys. Hugo's sentence shows how Javert ranks duty above blood.
quote: if she had broken her ban

text: Vidocq (1775–1857) was the escaped convict who became chief of the Paris detective police; Brutus the Roman consul who condemned his own sons for treason. Hugo means a policeman with a Roman's pitiless virtue.
quote: Brutus in Vidocq

text: In Greek myth, the river of the underworld that the dead cross and cannot recross. Hugo's image is of a law that places such a river at the bottom of society, so that those who fall can never come back.
quote: who place a Styx at the base of society

text: A gold coin. Strictly the louis was the old royal coin, but by the 1820s people used 'louis' for any twenty-franc gold piece, the same coin as the napoleon. Twenty louis, the four hundred francs Madeleine offers for lifting the cart, is more than a labourer earned in a year.
quote: There are five louis d’or to be earned!

text: A notaire was a public lawyer who drew up contracts, wills and property deeds and kept them on record; every small town had one, and he was a man of standing. An ex-notary reduced to driving a cart has fallen a long way.
quote: an ex-notary and a peasant who was almost educated

text: A blacksmith who shod horses and did rough ironwork. He was the likeliest person in a village to own a jackscrew, the screw-jack for lifting a cart.
quote: where there is a farrier

text: The Daughters of Charity, founded by Saint Vincent de Paul in 1633, were nuns who lived in the world rather than behind convent walls, nursing in hospitals and serving the poor in their grey-blue habit and great white cornette. Most French hospitals and infirmaries were staffed by them.
quote: served by two sisters of charity

text: Bank of France notes came only in large denominations, 500 and 1,000 francs, and ordinary people rarely saw one. A thousand francs was two or three years' wages for a working man.
quote: a thousand-franc banknote on his night-stand

text: A French mayor's badge of office is a sash worn across the chest or round the waist, put on for ceremonies and acts of authority. Seeing Madeleine in it is what makes Javert shudder.
quote: clothed in the scarf which gave him authority

text: Joseph de Villèle, the Ultra-royalist leader who was finance minister from 1821 and prime minister from 1822 to 1828. He was a careful administrator, and Hugo has him cite the arrondissement's cheap tax collection as a model.
quote: M. de Villèle, then Minister of Finance

text: The écrivain public sat at a stall or in a booth and wrote letters, petitions and love notes for the many who could not write. He knew everyone's secrets, which is why the gossips stand him drinks.
quote: she was obliged to write through a public letter-writer

term: paid the carriage on the letter
text: Before postage stamps, which France adopted only in 1849, postage was charged by distance and usually paid by the person who received the letter. Paying it in advance yourself was a courtesy, and an expense, which the workroom notices.
quote: she paid the carriage on the letter

term: from the Bernardines to the Jacobins
text: A pun. The Bernardines were Cistercian monks; the 'Jacobins' were Dominican friars, but also the radical revolutionary club named after their old convent in Paris. Madame Victurnien's husband left his monastery in 1793 for revolutionary politics.
quote: passed from the Bernardines to the Jacobins

text: In older English and in French (bigote), a person of showy, narrow and censorious piety, not specifically one prejudiced against a group. Madame Victurnien turned devout at the Restoration, when piety was in fashion and in favour.
quote: At the Restoration she had turned bigot

text: Sewing coarse shirts for the garrison brought in twelve sous, barely half a franc, for a long day; Cosette's board alone cost ten. When prison workshops undercut the trade, the rate falls to nine sous for seventeen hours. Hugo gives the arithmetic so the reader can see there is no way out.
quote: earned twelve sous a day

text: Hapgood's English for the liard, a tiny old copper coin worth a quarter of a sou. Half a farthing's worth of millet every two days is the cost of keeping a bird, and Fantine gives it up.
quote: half a farthing’s worth of millet

text: The gold twenty-franc piece first struck under Napoleon and still called by his name. Two napoleons make forty francs, the sum the Thénardiers demand and the dentist offers for two teeth.
quote: That makes two napoleons!

text: An old diagnosis for a feverish illness with a rash of tiny blisters like millet seeds, often fatal and much feared. Doctors of the time used it loosely; for the Thénardiers it is simply a frightening name.
quote: A miliary fever, they call it

text: Itinerant tooth-pullers worked fairs and market squares from a showy cart, selling elixirs and extracting teeth in public. Real human teeth were bought from the poor to make dentures for the rich, which is why he will pay for healthy front teeth.
quote: He was a quack dentist on his rounds

text: A euphemism for a prostitute (fille publique). Prostitution was legal but regulated: women were registered with the police and subject to their discretion. Hugo's next chapter calls it a form of slavery.
quote: The unfortunate girl became a woman of the town.

text: Latin, 'Christ has set us free', echoing Galatians 5:1. Hugo gives the title to his short sermon on prostitution as the slavery Christian Europe has not abolished.

Hugo's portrait of the provincial idler of 1823: three waistcoats, a short olive coat with a 'codfish tail', spurs without a horse and a fierce moustache. Pont-à-Mousson, a small town in Lorraine, stands for the provinces copying Paris copying London.
quote: They are dandies

text: Hats named after the two sides in the Spanish American wars of independence: Morillo was the royalist Spanish general, Bolívar the liberator. In France the narrow-brimmed 'morillo' marked a royalist, the broad 'bolivar' a liberal.
quote: and were called morillos

text: Hapgood's rendering of 'bien pensant': conventionally right-minded, loyal to throne and altar. Hugo uses it with sarcasm for the respectable man who torments Fantine.
quote: a “right thinker,”

text: Running the gauntlet: a soldier condemned to pass between two lines of comrades who beat him with rods, a punishment of the old armies. Fantine's silent circuit past the dandy is that ordeal repeated every five minutes.
quote: like the condemned soldier who returns under the rods

text: Under the Restoration only men paying at least 300 francs a year in direct taxes could vote, under a hundred thousand in all France. To Javert, M. Bamatabois as 'a freeholder and an elector' is society itself.
quote: in the person of a freeholder and an elector

text: The Code d'instruction criminelle of 1808, Napoleon's code of criminal procedure. Madeleine cites its articles, and a law of December 1799 against arbitrary detention, to show that minor street offences belong to the mayor's municipal police, so the decision is his, not the inspector's.
quote: of the code of criminal examination

text: Russian infantry were famous in the Napoleonic wars for standing and taking fire without flinching or breaking. Javert absorbs the mayor's order the same way.
quote: like a Russian soldier

text: René Laënnec (1781–1826), the French physician who invented the stethoscope in 1816 and described the signs of tuberculosis of the lungs, then called consumption or phthisis. Sounding a patient's chest was new medicine in 1823.
quote: the fine Laënnec’s fine suggestions

text: Christ's parable in Matthew 25 of the ten bridesmaids, five who kept their lamps filled and five who did not. Medieval sculptors carved them on cathedral portals, as at Reims. The 'ambubajae' were Syrian flute girls of ancient Rome, a byword for loose women.
quote: the wise virgins as they survey the foolish virgins

text: The headquarters of the Paris police, under the prefect of police, which also kept the national registers of convicts and wanted men. A provincial inspector's report on a suspect went there.
quote: At the Prefecture of Police in Paris

text: An assistant warder (adjudant) in the convict prison, a junior officer over the galley-sergeants. It means Javert knew the convicts of Toulon by sight, year after year.
quote: when I was adjutant-guard of convicts at Toulon

text: The chief town of the Pas-de-Calais, about twenty leagues east of Montreuil-sur-Mer, seat of the département's prefecture, its prison and its Court of Assizes. Robespierre came from there.
quote: where the departmental prison is situated

text: Convict slang for a convict or ex-convict, from the bundles of sticks that were tied together as the chained men were. Brevet, a former convict made turnkey, uses the galleys' own word.
quote: He is a fagot!

text: The juge d'instruction, the judge who investigates a criminal case before trial, questions the accused and witnesses, and decides whether to send it to court. He arranges the confrontations with men who claim to recognise the prisoner.
quote: the examining magistrate finds it convenient

text: French law punished a repeat offender far more heavily than a first offender. A theft of apples that would bring a few days in prison would, from a released convict, be housebreaking before the Assizes, punishable by the galleys for life.
quote: he has his previous conviction against him

text: The mountainous province of central France, whose people were known for migrating to Paris as water-carriers and labourers, and for an accent that turns 'Jean' into 'Chan'. Javert's theory of the name 'Champmathieu' depends on it.
quote: The local pronunciation turns Jean into Chan

text: Religious orders: Capuchins were barefoot, bearded Franciscan friars; Ursulines teaching nuns; Carmelites strictly enclosed contemplative nuns. Hugo lists them to say that the cloister easily absorbs a peasant's piety.
quote: a Capuchin or an Ursuline

text: Abbé Sicard (1742–1822) directed the Paris institute for the deaf; Jean Massieu was his famous deaf pupil and assistant. Hugo's mention of a letter praising Sister Simplice is a piece of invented authority, of the kind he enjoys.
quote: The Abbé Sicard speaks of Sister Simplice

text: The saint Hugo describes, martyred rather than tell a small lie about her birthplace, is not in the calendar of saints; he invented or adapted her to fit Sister Simplice's one rule, never to lie.
quote: Simplice of Sicily, as we know

text: A Flemish-speaking native of Flanders, the region straddling northern France and Belgium. Montreuil-sur-Mer is near enough for a Flemish horse-hirer; his Dutch-sounding name Scaufflaer is Frenchified as Scaufflaire.
quote: to a Fleming named Master Scaufflaer

text: Light two-wheeled carriages pulled by one horse. A cabriolet had a folding hood; a tilbury, named after its London maker, was lighter and faster still but open to the weather. In winter that is a real hardship.
quote: a little tilbury that I own

text: Main roads were divided into stages between post-houses, where travellers could change horses. Distances were reckoned in leagues between relays: here five to Hesdin, six to Saint-Pol, eight and a half to Arras.
quote: That must designate the posting relays

text: Small towns of the Pas-de-Calais on the road east from Montreuil-sur-Mer toward Arras. Hesdin was a fortified town on the Canche; Saint-Pol-sur-Ternoise a market town on the plateau.
quote: It is five leagues from here to Hesdin

text: Dante Alighieri, whose Inferno begins with the poet lost in a dark wood and brought to the gate of Hell. Hugo opens his chapter on a single night of conscience by setting it beside Homer's battles, Milton's demons and Dante's circles.
quote: Alighieri one day met with a sinister-looking door

text: Restoration elections were held by small colleges of wealthy voters who travelled to the chief town of the arrondissement or département to vote, often with a passport for the journey. That the mayor went 'to the elections' shows he counted among the few with the vote.
quote: when he went to the elections

text: The legend of the Wandering Jew, Ahasuerus, who mocked Christ on the way to Calvary and was condemned to walk the earth until the Second Coming, driven on by the command 'Walk!' Hugo likens the inner voice that will not let his man stop thinking to that curse.
quote: as it said to another condemned man, two thousand years ago, “March on!”

term: the iron necklet, the green cap
text: Galley dress distinguished terms of sentence: a red cap for a fixed term, a green cap for life. The iron collar (carcan) and the 'post' were the public exposure in the pillory that preceded a convict's departure for the galleys, abolished in 1832.
quote: the iron necklet, the green cap

text: Travaux forcés à perpétuité, hard labour for life in the bagne. Under the Penal Code a man already sentenced to hard labour who committed a new crime could receive it, which is why a second theft by an ex-convict, however small, is so dangerous.
quote: penal servitude for life
