text: A village with a wood on the heights east of Paris, a favourite Sunday spot for lovers gathering lilac in spring. The name surfaces in the man's exhausted mind from a clock-maker's name and an old song, the sort of stray memory a mind seizes on in extremity.
quote: Romainville was a little grove near Paris

text: Christ's agony in the garden of Gethsemane among the olive trees, where he prayed that 'this cup' of suffering might pass from him (Matthew 26:39). Hugo ends the chapter by setting the night's struggle against that one.
quote: the terrible cup which appeared to Him

text: Hugo's narrator presents himself as a historian working from documents, here a written account of a dream left by the man himself. It is a novelist's device for authority and intimacy, like his references to witnesses still alive.
quote: It is one of the papers in his own handwriting

text: The malle-poste, the light, fast government coach that carried the mails at night between towns, with one or two seats for passengers. Hugo describes the old two-wheeled Empire model, yellow with a black mail-box behind.
quote: small mail-wagons of the time of the Empire

text: A calèche, a low four-wheeled carriage with a folding hood, needing two horses. A wheelwright in a poor town is keeping one for a townsman who uses it 'on the thirty-sixth of the month', a French joke for never.
quote: an old calash under the shed yonder

text: Fresh horses hired at each posting station along a main road, with a postilion to bring them back. They were the fastest way to travel, but on a crossroad in ploughing season the relays might have no horses to give, and a passport had to be shown.
quote: I will take two post-horses

text: The rider who sits on one of the horses, or here on the shaft, to drive and guide, then takes the horses back to their relay. The stable-boy calls himself one to sound grander.
quote: who called himself a postilion

text: The swinging crossbar to which a horse's traces are hitched, so that its pull reaches the cart evenly. If it breaks, the horse cannot draw at all; a cut branch can stand in for it.
quote: the whiffletree broke

text: Villages of the Artois plain on the way to Arras. Mont-Saint-Éloy is marked by the ruined towers of its old abbey on a hill north-west of the city. The detour by Carency and Camblin is through real country lanes.
quote: towards Tinques, which is only five leagues from Arras

text: The canopy over a curtained bed. Hospital beds, like domestic ones, were often hung with curtains for warmth and privacy, which is why Fantine has to push her head through them to listen.
quote: staring at the tester of her bed

text: Cinchona or Peruvian bark, the source of quinine, the standard remedy for fevers. An infusion of it was among the few things a doctor of 1823 could prescribe for a consumptive's fever.
quote: an infusion of pure chinchona

text: Fantine's lullaby, with its refrain of pink roses and blue cornflowers and the Virgin bringing linen for a baby, is Hugo's own pastiche of an old French folk romance. Its last turn, from baby clothes to a winding-sheet, is in the folk tradition.
quote: This song was an old cradle romance

text: A carriage gateway: a large door opening from the street into an inner courtyard, wide enough for a coach. Inns and town houses had them.
quote: entered the porte-cochère of the Hotel de la Poste

text: Cheval de retour, slang for a convict who has come back, a repeat offender. It was originally a post-horse being taken back to its home stable. The lawyers in the hall use it as casually as 'old lag'.
quote: the “return horse.”

text: A woman from the Limousin, in central France. Infanticide by poor unmarried mothers was one of the commonest capital cases at the Assizes; juries often refused to find premeditation, which brought the sentence down from death to hard labour for life.
quote: The Limosin woman

text: The prefect's official residence and offices. At Arras it occupied the former bishop's palace, confiscated in the Revolution, and while the courthouse was repaired the Assizes sat in its great hall, under the old episcopal ceilings.
quote: the prefecture of today was the bishop’s palace before the Revolution

text: The presiding judge of the Court of Assizes, a councillor of the Royal Court (the appeal court) sent to preside over the session. He questioned the accused and witnesses himself and summed up for the jury; places behind his chair were for privileged spectators.
quote: behind Monsieur le President

text: The huissier audiencier, the court officer who kept the doors, called witnesses and carried messages to the bench. His sudden deference shows what a mayor's name is worth.
quote: An usher stood at the door

text: The cour royale was the regional appeal court; Douai's covered the Nord and the Pas-de-Calais. One of its councillors presided over each quarterly session of the Assizes in the département.
quote: The Councillor of the Royal Court of Douai

text: The commune is the basic unit of French local government, a town or village with its own mayor. The arrondissement of Montreuil-sur-Mer had about a hundred and forty of them.
quote: the hundred and forty communes

text: Jean-Nicolas Pache was minister of war and then mayor of Paris during the Terror. The framed letter, dated in the revolutionary calendar, is about the arrest of deputies in 1793: a relic of the Revolution's own justice hanging in the judges' room.
quote: Jean Nicolas Pache, mayor of Paris

text: The article of the 1810 Penal Code that punished theft on a public highway with hard labour for life, and with death in aggravated cases. That is why the prosecutor 'reserves' the earlier robbery of the boy for a later trial.
quote: article 383 of the Penal Code

text: Two small, sleepy provincial towns, used here as Hugo uses Pont-à-Mousson: anywhere far from Paris. He mocks the stately periphrases of courtroom oratory, where a theatre is 'the temple of Melpomene', the Muse of tragedy.
quote: at Romorantin or at Montbrison

text: In his funeral oration for Anne of Gonzaga, the great preacher Bossuet had to describe a dream in which a hen protected her chicks, and did it in grand style. Hugo cites it to excuse the defence lawyer's lofty treatment of stolen apples.
quote: Bénigne Bossuet himself was obliged to allude to a chicken

text: The poet Robert Southey's sneer (1821) at Byron and Shelley, taken up by French conservative critics against the young Romantics, Hugo among them. The Quotidienne and the Oriflamme were royalist papers. The prosecutor blames the crime on Romantic literature, a fashionable charge.
quote: The Satanic School

text: In Racine's tragedy 'Phèdre', Théramène delivers a long, famous speech describing the sea monster that kills Hippolyte. Its set-piece horror, Hugo says, is the model for prosecutors' portraits of the accused as monsters.
quote: the tale of Théramène

text: A man sentenced to an 'ignominious' penalty, such as hard labour, lost his civil rights, including the right to testify under oath. Convicts could be heard only 'for information', which is why the President appeals to their conscience instead.
quote: you cannot take an oath

text: The maisons centrales, large prisons created under Napoleon for men serving long terms of 'reclusion' rather than hard labour, with their own grey-and-black uniform. Their workshops produced goods under contract, the 'prison work' that undercut seamstresses' wages.
quote: the black and gray waistcoat of the central prisons

text: Paris washerwomen worked on floating laundry-boats on the Seine or in covered washhouses like that of the Enfants-Rouges, standing in tubs or bending over running water all day in every season. It was one of the hardest and worst-paid trades for women.
quote: my daughter, who was a laundress at the river

text: Mardi Gras, the last day of Carnival before Lent, when Paris went masked to balls and street festivities. A working girl who went to bed at eight that night was very sober indeed.
quote: one Shrove-Tuesday

text: Travaux Forcés à Perpétuité, hard labour for life. Until 1832 convicts were branded on the shoulder with a hot iron bearing the letters of their sentence, and some tried to burn the mark away. The brand stayed for life.
quote: the three letters T. F. P.

text: Hugo, writing around 1860, claims that the speech was written down by a witness and still rings in the ears of those who heard it. The narrator's pose as a chronicler of real events with surviving witnesses gives the scene the weight of testimony.
quote: nearly forty years ago

text: Doctors held a small mirror to a patient's lips to see whether it misted, the simplest test of whether breath, and so life, remained. It is the only looking-glass in the sisters' infirmary.
quote: the little glass which the doctor of the infirmary used to see whether a patient was dead

text: French Catholic children made their first communion at about twelve, after catechism classes, girls dressed in white with a veil like little brides. It was a great family occasion and a mark of respectability. Fantine counts the years until her daughter's.
quote: Then she will take her first communion

text: An epiphonema is a rhetorical flourish, a sententious exclamation that rounds off an argument. Hugo means that the defence lawyer closed with stock lines about judicial error.
quote: some epiphonemas, not very fresh

text: Under the Restoration, calling Napoleon 'the Emperor' implied that his reign had been legitimate; loyal royalists said 'Bonaparte' or 'the usurper'. A single word in a speech could betray a man's politics, and here it shocks the royalist President.
quote: say the Emperor, and not Bonaparte

text: A stiff band of leather or cloth worn round the neck in place of a cravat, buckled at the back, part of military and police dress. A buckle slipped round under the ear is, for a man as exact as Javert, a sign of inner upheaval.
quote: The buckle of his leather stock was under his left ear

text: The archangel who leads the armies of heaven and is shown with his foot on the dragon, sword raised, weighing souls. Hugo's 'monstrous Saint Michael' is righteousness without mercy.
quote: this monstrous Saint Michael

text: The poucettes were small screw-clamps fastened on a prisoner's thumbs to control him under arrest, a police tool rather than a torture here. Javert threatens them to hurry his man away.
quote: or you’ll get the thumbscrews!

text: 'The White Flag', an Ultra-royalist newspaper of the Restoration, named after the Bourbon flag. Its old lady subscriber turns the mayor's fall into a lesson for Bonapartists, though nothing connects them.
quote: a subscriber to the Drapeau Blanc

text: The loose smock of blue or grey linen worn over other clothes by French workmen, carters and peasants. It was the uniform of the labouring class, and a perfect disguise for a man leaving a town on foot.
quote: he was dressed in a blouse

text: The fosse commune, a shared trench in the cemetery where the poor were buried free, without a marked plot, the bodies laid side by side and the ground reused after some years. A paid concession was needed for a grave of one's own.
quote: She was thrown into the public grave.

text: The narrator steps out of the story as himself: Hugo really did visit the battlefield in May 1861, staying at Mont-Saint-Jean while he finished the novel. Volume II opens with a traveller's walk, not with the characters.
quote: Last year (1861), on a beautiful May morning

text: Towns of Belgian Brabant just south of Brussels, at the western edge of the battlefield. In 1815 Belgium was part of the new Kingdom of the Netherlands; the field lies along the roads from Nivelles and from Genappe to Brussels.
quote: was coming from Nivelles

text: A walled château-farm with a garden and orchard on the western side of the field of Waterloo. The French attacked it all day and never took it from its British Guards and German defenders. Hugo walks into it as a working farm, still scarred by shot.
quote: “Hougomont,” said the peasant woman.

text: The Lion's Mound, an artificial hill about forty metres high topped by a cast-iron lion, raised in 1826 by the Dutch king where his son the Prince of Orange was wounded. Building it reshaped the ground, as Hugo complains: the field is no longer as it was.
quote: something which at that distance resembled a lion

text: A village about fifteen kilometres south of Brussels, where Wellington had his headquarters and dated his dispatch. The fighting took place a few kilometres further south, around Mont-Saint-Jean, but the battle took the village's name.
quote: He was on the battlefield of Waterloo.

text: Light companies of the British Foot Guards under General Cooke, who held Hougomont with Nassau and Hanoverian troops against repeated French assaults. The defence of its north gate, forced and then shut again, became a British legend.
quote: Cooke’s four companies of guards

text: Jérôme Bonaparte, the Emperor's youngest brother and former King of Westphalia, who commanded a division in Reille's corps. His attack on Hougomont, meant as a diversion, swallowed thousands of men. Foy, Bachelu, Guilleminot and Kellermann were French generals in the same sector.
quote: Napoleon sent his brother Jérôme against Hougomont

text: Wellington's army was barely a third British: the rest were Dutch and Belgian troops and contingents from German states, Hanover (ruled by the British king), the duchy of Nassau and the duchy of Brunswick, whose black-uniformed soldiers had lost their duke two days earlier.
quote: the Hanoverian lieutenant, Wilda

text: A heavy musket ball, or a large lead ball fired from a cannon in a case of grapeshot, named after the long Biscay muskets. Grapeshot and canister were clusters of small balls that scattered from the gun's mouth like a giant shotgun.
quote: its bullet or its biscayan

text: André Le Nôtre (1613–1700), the gardener of Versailles, master of the formal French garden. Hougomont's terraced garden is in the older style before him, and in 1861 ruins and briars.
quote: the first French style which preceded Lenôtre

text: Henri IV's edict of 1598 granting French Protestants freedom of worship. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685 and hundreds of thousands of Huguenots fled abroad, which is how the German general Duplat came to have a French name.
quote: the revocation of the Edict of Nantes

text: Gebhard von Blücher (1742–1819), the seventy-two-year-old Prussian field marshal, beaten by Napoleon at Ligny two days before Waterloo but able to march to Wellington's aid. Hugo makes the late start of the battle, caused by the rain, the reason he arrived in time.
quote: that gave Blücher time to come up

text: Napoleon's greatest victory, over the Austrians and Russians on 2 December 1805, where the morning 'sun of Austerlitz' broke through the fog. Hugo uses it as Waterloo's opposite: the beginning and the end of the Empire's glory.
quote: make Waterloo the end of Austerlitz

text: Napoleon trained as a gunner and first made his name directing the guns at the siege of Toulon in 1793. Massed artillery was the key to his battles, so ground too wet for the guns to move was a serious handicap.
quote: Napoleon was an artillery officer

text: Towns west and east of Brussels, the directions of the British and Prussian lines of retreat. Napoleon's plan was to split the two allied armies and drive them apart toward their own bases.
quote: to drive the British half back on Hal

text: A hamlet and farm on the Brussels road where the ground rises to a plateau. Wellington's army stood along its crest, partly hidden behind it, which is why the French called the battle after it. Hugo's capital A puts it at the apex.
quote: The top of the A is Mont-Saint-Jean

text: An inn on the Brussels road south of the plateau, near Napoleon's position. Its name, 'the fine alliance', struck Hugo as an omen, since Wellington and Blücher met there after the battle; the Prussians wanted the battle named after it.
quote: the right tip is the Belle-Alliance, where Napoleon was

text: A sunken lane running along the crest of the plateau from Braine-l'Alleud to Ohain, cut deep between banks, invisible from the French side. The building of the Lion's Mound later used its banks and levelled it. Hugo describes it with dread.
quote: the hollow road to Ohain from Braine-l’Alleud

text: The great beech forest that runs between the battlefield and Brussels. It lay at Wellington's back, so a defeat would have meant a disorderly retreat through its tracks and ponds.
quote: is the forest of Soignes

text: The military school at Brienne-le-Château in Champagne where the young Bonaparte studied from 1779 to 1784. Hugo dresses the Emperor in his famous costume: little cocked hat, green chasseur's coat, the sword he carried at Marengo.
quote: the little three-cornered hat of the school of Brienne

text: Sir Thomas Picton and Lord Hill were Wellington's veteran generals from the Spanish campaigns; Picton was killed in the battle. D'Erlon and Reille were the French corps commanders facing them.
quote: d’Erlon facing Picton, Reille facing Hill

text: Hugo lists conquerors whose glory is diminished by what they did: Alexander the Great at Babylon, Caesar enslaving Rome, Titus destroying Jerusalem in AD 70. History, he says, sets the despot against the hero in the same man.
quote: Babylon violated lessens Alexander

text: A walled farm in front of the centre of Wellington's line, on the Brussels road, held by the King's German Legion until they ran out of ammunition and it fell in the late afternoon. It was the key to the British centre.
quote: hurling Quiot’s brigade on La Haie-Sainte

text: Michel Ney (1769–1815), marshal of France, 'the bravest of the brave', who directed the French attacks at Waterloo. He had promised Louis XVIII to bring Napoleon back 'in an iron cage' and then went over to him in March 1815.
quote: Ney pushed forward the right wing

text: Latin, 'something obscure, something divine', Hugo's tag for the element in a battle that escapes plans and maps. The chapter's title calls it the 'quid obscurum' of battles.
quote: Quid obscurum, quid divinum.

text: Salvator Rosa was a seventeenth-century painter of wild battle scenes; Gribeauval the eighteenth-century engineer who standardised French artillery. Rembrandt and Van der Meulen, Folard and Polybius are paired the same way: the painter of chaos against the exact recorder.
quote: what Salvator Rosa requires, not what is suited to the needs of Gribeauval

text: The Royal Scots Greys, a heavy cavalry regiment on grey horses, part of Ponsonby's Union Brigade. Their charge broke d'Erlon's infantry early in the afternoon, then ran on too far and was cut up by French lancers and cuirassiers.
quote: The Scotch Grays no longer existed

text: William, heir to the Dutch throne, aged twenty-two, who commanded Wellington's Dutch-Belgian corps and was wounded in the battle. The Lion's Mound marks the spot.
quote: The Prince of Orange was in command of the centre

text: Wellington's victories over the French in Spain during the Peninsular War (1808–1814). His 'old companions' were the veterans of those campaigns.
quote: his old companions of Talavera, of Vittoria, of Salamanca

text: Latin, 'Caesar laughs, Pompey will weep', a soldiers' saying before Pharsalus, where Caesar beat Pompey. Hugo applies it to Napoleon's high spirits on the morning of Waterloo, then reverses it.
quote: Ridet Caesar, Pompeius flebit

text: The famous ball in Brussels on the night of 15 June 1815, where Wellington and his officers learned that Napoleon had crossed the frontier; many went straight from the dance to battle. Soult's joke at breakfast turns on it.
quote: at the Duchess of Richmond’s

text: Nicolas Soult, marshal of France and Duke of Dalmatia, Napoleon's chief of staff in 1815. He had fought Wellington for years in Spain and warned the Emperor not to underrate him.
quote: saying to Soult as he did so

text: The grognards, Napoleon's nickname for the veteran grenadiers of the Old Guard, who grumbled on the march but followed him anywhere. It became the name for any old soldier of the Empire.
quote: his grenadiers “his grumblers;”

text: The small Mediterranean island off Tuscany given to Napoleon as a sovereign principality after his first abdication in 1814. He escaped from it in February 1815 on the brig L'Inconstant and landed in France on 1 March.
quote: trip from the island of Elba to France

text: Latin, 'with rough rust', from Virgil's Georgics, where the farmer of the future ploughs up rusted spears and helmets on an old battlefield. Hugo, turning up shell fragments on the knoll, is that farmer.
quote: Scabra rubigine

text: Emmanuel de Grouchy, the marshal sent with some 30,000 men to pursue the Prussians after Ligny. He followed his orders too literally, ignored the sound of the guns and never reached the field: the absent army of Waterloo.
quote: Grouchy’s delay

text: The disasters of Napoleon's decline: the river crossing during the retreat from Moscow in 1812, the 'Battle of the Nations' lost in 1813, and the palace where he abdicated in April 1814. Crécy, Poitiers, Agincourt, Malplaquet and Ramillies are old English victories over France.
quote: when one has Bérésina, Leipzig, and Fontainebleau behind one

text: Napoleon's victory over the Austrians in northern Italy in June 1800, which secured his power as First Consul. 'The man of Marengo' is the young Bonaparte of the glory years.
quote: The man of Marengo was wiping out Agincourt

text: Heavy cavalry who wore a steel breastplate (cuirass) and helmet, on big horses, used to break enemy lines by sheer weight. Milhaud's and Kellermann's cuirassiers made the great charges of the afternoon.
quote: He gave orders to Milhaud’s cuirassiers

text: The battle of Borodino, near Moscow, on 7 September 1812, which the French call the Moskova. The heavy cavalry took the great redoubt there, under Murat, Napoleon's flamboyant cavalry marshal and brother-in-law.
quote: the great redoubt of the Muskowa

text: Against cavalry, infantry formed hollow squares several ranks deep, bayonets outward on every side, the front rank kneeling. Horses would not charge into a steady wall of bayonets, and the guns sheltered inside. Wellington's squares stood all afternoon.
quote: the English infantry, formed into thirteen squares

text: 'Long live the Emperor!', the battle-cry of Napoleon's armies. After 1815 shouting it in France was a 'seditious cry' that could bring a prison sentence.
quote: shouting, “Vive l’Empereur!”

text: Strictly the classical music of the Highland bagpipe, but here the pipes themselves. Scottish regiments marched and fought to them. 'Ben Lothian' is Hugo's invented Scottish mountain.
quote: with his pibroch under his arm

text: The Duke of Wellington (1769–1852), Arthur Wellesley, commander of the allied army. 'Blücher, or night!' is his famous prayer: either the Prussians arrive or darkness ends the fighting.
quote: The Iron Duke remained calm

text: During the Hundred Days the king and his court took refuge in Ghent, in Belgium, waiting on the outcome. The panic among fugitives from the battlefield reached them there; the Prince de Condé was at Mechlin.
quote: the Prince de Condé at Mechlin, and Louis XVIII at Ghent

text: Friedrich Wilhelm von Bülow, commander of Blücher's IV Corps, the first Prussian troops to reach the field. His attack on Plancenoit, behind Napoleon's right, drew off the French reserves.
quote: Bülow, Blücher’s lieutenant

text: A village behind the French right, where the arriving Prussians struck. It changed hands several times in savage fighting between Prussians and the Young Guard, and burned.
quote: instead of below Plancenoit

text: The Imperial Guard, Napoleon's elite reserve of veterans in tall bearskin caps, his last card at Waterloo. Its repulse on the slope of Mont-Saint-Jean in the evening, the first time it had been beaten, set off the French collapse.
quote: the Guard entering the line

text: The highest military dignity in France, revived by Napoleon. Hugo's 'reserved for French bullets' refers to Ney's fate: tried by the Chamber of Peers and shot by a firing squad in Paris in December 1815 for rallying to Napoleon.
quote: how a Marshal of France dies on the field of battle!

text: Lancers of the Prussian and other German armies. In the pursuit after the battle they, and the Prussian 'death's-head' hussars with skulls on their caps, gave no quarter.
quote: the swords of the Uhlans

text: La Grande Armée, the name of Napoleon's main army from 1805, which had marched from Madrid to Moscow. Hugo ends the rout with the name, to measure the fall.
quote: The Grand Army.

text: Latin, 'this was in the fates': it was destined. Hugo's view is that Waterloo was decided by Providence, not by generals.
quote: Hoc erat in fatis.

text: Napoleon's victories of 1805–1809, over Austria (Ulm, Wagram), Prussia (Jena) and Russia (Friedland). The last squares of the Guard, Hugo says, carried those names down with them.
quote: Ulm, Wagram, Jéna, Friedland, died with them

text: General Pierre Cambronne (1770–1842), who commanded a battalion of the Old Guard in the last squares. Called on to surrender, he is said to have answered either 'The Guard dies but does not surrender' or the single word Hugo prints. He was wounded, captured, and survived.
quote: an obscure officer named Cambronne

text: 'Shit!', the coarsest common French word, which Hugo was the first to print in a serious novel, and defends at length in the next chapter. French speakers still call it 'le mot de Cambronne', Cambronne's word.
quote: Cambronne replied, “Merde!”

text: Leonidas was the Spartan king who died holding the pass of Thermopylae; Rabelais the earthy comic genius of the French Renaissance. To finish one with the other is Hugo's summary of Cambronne's answer: heroism and obscenity in one breath.
quote: to finish Leonidas with Rabellais

text: Claude-Joseph Rouget de Lisle, the army officer who wrote the 'Marseillaise' in a single night in 1792. Danton, the great orator of the Revolution, and Kléber, a republican general, are Hugo's other examples of that spirit.
quote: as Rouget invents the “Marseillaise,”

text: Jean-Baptiste Charras, a republican colonel exiled after Louis-Napoleon's coup of 1851, like Hugo, and author of a careful history of the 1815 campaign that Hugo used. Jomini and Müffling were earlier military historians of the battle.
quote: Charras alone

text: In the old French state lottery, a 'quine' was the jackpot won by drawing all five numbers. Waterloo, for Hugo, was a lucky draw: 'won by Europe, paid by France'.
quote: The quine won by Europe, paid by France.

text: François Barrême, a seventeenth-century mathematician whose book of ready-reckoned tables gave French the word 'barème', a scale of figures. Calling Wellington the Barrême of war and Napoleon its Michelangelo sets calculation against genius.
quote: Wellington was the Barême of war

text: Bonaparte's victories in his first Italian campaign of 1796–1797, when at twenty-six he beat a series of elderly Austrian generals: Beaulieu, Wurmser, Alvinczy. Hugo's quip is that Wellington is simply a Wurmser who won.
quote: beneath Lodi, Montebello, Montenotte, Mantua, Arcola

text: On 20 March 1815 Napoleon re-entered Paris and the Tuileries, the night after Louis XVIII fled. With the 14th of July 1789, the storming of the Bastille, it stands for Hugo as revolutionary France, which the allies at Waterloo were fighting.
quote: attacked through the 20th of March, 1815

term: a postilion on the throne of Naples
text: Napoleon made Joachim Murat, an innkeeper's son, King of Naples, and his marshal Bernadotte, once a sergeant, became Crown Prince and then King of Sweden. Hugo's point is that the Empire, despotic as it was, spread the Revolution's equality.
quote: Bonaparte places a postilion on the throne of Naples

text: General Maximilien Foy, wounded at Waterloo, became the great liberal orator of the Chamber of Deputies under the Restoration; his funeral in 1825 was a huge opposition demonstration. Hugo's example of a soldier turned into a voice for liberty.
quote: Foy falls at Hougomont and rises again in the tribune

text: Henri IV (reigned 1589–1610), the first Bourbon king, born in Béarn, a popular hero of the monarchy. The Restoration set him up as the anti-Napoleon: 'the Corsican' against 'the Bearnese'.
quote: The Corsican became the antithesis of the Bearnese

text: Hartwell House in Buckinghamshire, England, where Louis XVIII lived in exile from 1808 to 1814. Hugo pictures the exile's simple pine table carried into the throne room of Louis XIV.
quote: Hartwell’s pine table

text: The nickname of Jacques Dupont, leader of royalist gangs who murdered Protestants and Bonapartists around Nîmes in the 'White Terror' of 1815. That he 'was celebrated' says what the new order tolerated.
quote: Trestaillon was celebrated.

text: Latin, 'not unequal to many', the motto of Louis XIV, set under his emblem of the sun. Its return on barrack walls marks the Restoration's revival of the old monarchy's symbols.
quote: The device non pluribus impar reappeared

text: A young Bourbon prince kidnapped from German territory on Napoleon's orders and shot in the moat of the château of Vincennes in March 1804, the year of the coronation. The Restoration raised a monument on the spot.
quote: the Duc d’Enghien had perished

text: The article of the Charter of 1814 that let the king issue ordinances 'for the security of the State'. Liberals feared it as a loophole for absolute rule; Hugo calls it the serpent hidden in the constitution.
quote: with Article 14 in the heart

text: The pact signed in September 1815 by the rulers of Russia, Austria and Prussia to govern by Christian principles, which in practice meant suppressing revolution in Europe. Hugo sets it against 'Belle-Alliance', the inn on the battlefield.
quote: There was a Holy Alliance

text: Sir Hudson Lowe, the British governor of St Helena and Napoleon's jailer, whose petty strictness became notorious. Montchenu was the French commissioner on the island; Longwood the damp house where Napoleon lived and died in 1821.
quote: England had him guarded by Hudson Lowe

text: The conference of European powers (1814–1815) that redrew the map after Napoleon's wars and restored the old dynasties. Hugo makes it, more than the return of the king, the true Restoration.
quote: The Congress of Vienna made the treaties in 1815

text: Latin, 'thus you, but not for yourselves', from a verse attributed to Virgil about a poet whose work another claimed. The village of Waterloo, which took no part, gets the glory of the fighting at Mont-Saint-Jean and Hougomont.
quote: the sic vos non vobis

text: The camp followers, deserters and hangers-on who trailed every army: sutlers selling drink and food from carts, servants, beggars, marauders. They stripped and robbed the dead and wounded after a battle, and soldiers caught doing the same could be shot.
quote: they are called “stragglers.”

text: A sutler (vivandier) sold provisions and drink to soldiers on campaign from a covered cart, often run by a man and his wife. The little wagon hidden by the Nivelles road is the kind that followed every army.
quote: a sort of little sutler’s wagon

text: The Vicomte de Turenne (1611–1675), Louis XIV's great marshal, loved by his men, who allowed them to pillage and devastated the Palatinate in 1674. Hoche and Marceau, young generals of the Republic, kept strict discipline.
quote: Turenne was adored by his soldiers

text: Hugo's name for night-wandering larvae or spirits of Norman folklore, creatures that haunt ruins. The image fits the furtive figure moving among the dead.
quote: which ancient Norman legends call the Alleurs

text: A Paris daily devoted to court reports, founded in 1825, which made trials a popular reading matter. Before it, news of a provincial case reached the public only in brief paragraphs like the two Hugo 'transcribes' from the Drapeau Blanc and the Journal de Paris.
quote: the Gazette des Tribunaux was not yet in existence

text: Voltaire, who spent his last twenty years at his château of Ferney near Geneva and was revered there as 'the patriarch'. The newspaper quotes his verse on the little Savoyards who come every year to sweep chimneys.
quote: the patriarch of Ferney

text: Only the king could pardon or commute a sentence. A death sentence reduced to hard labour for life was a common act of royal clemency, and the Constitutionnel, a liberal paper, read it as favour to a man known for his piety.
quote: has deigned to commute his penalty

text: When Alexander the Great died in 323 BC his generals carved his empire into rival kingdoms. Hugo compares the break-up of Madeleine's industry among squabbling former foremen to that partition.
quote: because it occurred after the death of Alexander

text: Hugo's account of a Montfermeil superstition: a horned black man digs holes in the forest at night to hide the devil's treasure, and whoever meets him dies within a week, a month or a year depending on what he does. Tryphon's Latin couplet lists what the digger finds: 'copper, coins, stones, a corpse, ghosts, and nothing'.
quote: the devil, from time immemorial, has selected the forest as a hiding-place

text: Roger Bacon, the thirteenth-century English friar, was credited with the first Western recipe for gunpowder; playing cards were said to have been invented to amuse the mad French king Charles VI around 1392. Hugo uses them to date the devil's later finds.
quote: before Roger Bacon’s time, and cards before the time of Charles VI

text: Cantonniers kept a stretch of road in repair, breaking stones by the roadside. The administration gave such work, at reduced pay, to released convicts under police supervision who could find nothing else, which is how Boulatruelle lives.
quote: employed him at reduced rates as a road-mender

text: Under the old monarchy, judicial torture ('the question') was used to extract confessions; one form forced quantities of water into the accused. It was abolished in 1788. Thénardier's 'wine test' is the tavern version.
quote: the water test, for example

text: Sceptics and anticlericals who mocked religion in Voltaire's manner, a familiar village type of the Restoration alongside the devout. Their jibe about catching the devil turns the superstition into a joke.
quote: The Voltairians added

text: In 1823 a French army under the Duc d'Angoulême invaded Spain at the request of the Holy Alliance to restore the absolute power of Ferdinand VII against the liberal constitution. It was quick and almost bloodless. Hugo calls it a war by Napoleon's generals for Louis XIV's heirs against liberty.
quote: “the epoch of the Spanish war.”

text: The Duc d'Angoulême, nephew of Louis XVIII, issued an ordinance at Andújar curbing royalist reprisals in Spain; the liberal papers gave him the title with irony. The Trocadéro was a fort at Cadiz whose capture ended the war, and gave its name to a square in Paris.
quote: “the hero of Andujar,”

text: The Spanish Inquisition, the church tribunal for heresy, abolished by the liberals and the symbol of the absolute monarchy that France was restoring. The 'descamisados', the shirtless, were the Spanish radicals, as the sans-culottes had been the French.
quote: the Holy Office

text: The Rhineland town where émigré nobles gathered an army against the Revolution in 1791–1792 under the white flag. In 1823 a few French liberals in Spain did the same under the tricolour, against their own country's army.
quote: thirty years earlier at Coblentz

text: The Spanish city whose people, led by General Palafox, held out against two terrible French sieges in 1808–1809. Rostopchin was the Moscow governor blamed for burning the city in 1812; Ballesteros a Spanish general who surrendered in 1823. France, Hugo says, prefers enemies who fight.
quote: Soldiers of the war of 1808, on whom Saragossa had fallen

text: Spanish, 'the king pure and simple': an absolute king without a constitution, the royalists' cry for Ferdinand VII. Hugo's warning is that a French government able to impose one in Madrid might be tempted to try at home.
quote: el rey netto

text: The manchineel, a tropical tree whose sap and fruit are poisonous; legend held that sleeping in its shade was fatal. Hugo's image for a regime trusting the loyalty of its army.
quote: in the shadow of a machineel tree

text: The largest class of sailing warship, with two or three gun decks and up to 120 cannon, built to fight in the line of battle. Convicts from the bagne worked in Toulon's naval arsenal and were sent aboard ships under repair.
quote: A ship of the line is one of the most magnificent combinations

text: A yard is the long horizontal spar from which a square sail hangs; sailors working the sail stood on a foot-rope slung beneath it. The topman is the sailor stationed aloft on the tops of the masts.
quote: he seized the footrope

text: Villages on either side of Montfermeil east of Paris, Chelles in the Marne valley with the remains of a royal abbey. The plateau between the Ourcq and the Marne was wooded and dry, so water had to be fetched from springs and ponds.
quote: Montfermeil is situated between Livry and Chelles

text: Christmas in rural France was a church feast with a midnight mass, a late supper and a fair, not a day of family presents; children set out a shoe by the hearth for a small gift. A travelling fair has set up its booths in the village for the feast.
quote: On Christmas eve itself

text: The optical toy of mirrors and coloured glass, invented by the Scot David Brewster in 1816 and a craze across Europe in the following years. With a ribbed tin lamp it dates the Thénardiers' room to 1823.
quote: a kaleidoscope and a lamp of ribbed tin

text: A whip of several knotted cords on a handle, used in armies and navies for flogging. Hanging on a nail in the chimney-corner, it is the household's instrument for one child only.
quote: a cat-o’-nine-tails was hanging on a nail

text: Sabots, shoes carved from a single block of wood, worn by peasants and the poor, often without stockings. Cosette wears them on bare feet in winter while she knits woollen stockings for the Thénardier girls.
quote: her bare feet were thrust into wooden shoes

text: Jacques Delille (1738–1813), a fashionable poet and translator of Virgil, admired in his day and soon ridiculed. Thénardier looks like his portraits; his heroes Voltaire, Raynal and Parny were all freethinking writers of the eighteenth century.
quote: the portraits of the Abbé Delille

text: A pun on 'filou' (swindler) and 'philosophe', the eighteenth-century name for the freethinking men of letters. Hugo's coinage for a cheat who talks like a philosopher.
quote: A filousophe, a scientific thief.

text: 'Field of Refuge', a colony founded in Texas in 1818 by exiled Bonapartist officers. Liberals and Bonapartists in France subscribed money for it, a safe political gesture; it collapsed within months.
quote: He had subscribed for the Champ d’Asile.

text: Slang for money, from a Latin legal phrase; 'to have the quibus' is to be in funds. Hugo names exactly where Thénardier's came from.
quote: “some quibus,”

text: A parliamentary phrase: to drag the monarch's name into public debate, which ministers were bound to avoid. Madame Thénardier never contradicts her husband 'before strangers'.
quote: “exposing the crown.”

text: A small silver coin worth three-quarters of a franc, enough for a large loaf. For Cosette it is a sum she is responsible for and cannot replace.
quote: Here’s a fifteen-sou piece.

text: The first mass of Christmas, celebrated at midnight on Christmas eve, to which villagers walked carrying candles. The fair's booths stay lit for them.
quote: on their way to the midnight mass

text: Country people believed in the loup-garou, a person turned wolf at night who roamed the fields. A small figure out alone in the dark on Christmas eve is, for a moment, uncanny.
quote: Is it a werewolf child?

text: A country name for a crimped wild grass, likened to the stiff pleated ruff worn at the court of Henri IV. Hugo gives the spring's plants their local names.
quote: those tall, crimped grasses which are called Henry IV’s frills

text: A wide, half-empty boulevard on the south-east edge of Paris, running past the vast Salpêtrière hospital for poor and insane women. The faubourg Saint-Marceau around it was one of the poorest quarters of the city.
quote: the Boulevard de l’Hôpital in Paris

text: A town on the Seine south of Paris with a royal château. Louis XVIII, too lame to walk, drove there almost daily at a gallop, so the poor women of the quarter told the time by his carriage.
quote: King Louis XVIII went nearly every day to Choisy-le-Roi

term: the Golden Fleece, the cross of Saint Louis
text: Royal orders of chivalry worn by Louis XVIII: the Habsburg and Spanish Order of the Golden Fleece, the military Order of Saint Louis, and the Order of the Holy Spirit with its wide blue ribbon, the highest order of the French monarchy. His hair is powdered in the style called 'royal bird'.
quote: the Golden Fleece, the cross of Saint Louis

text: The Gardes du Corps, the king's mounted household troops in silver-laced uniforms, restored in 1814. The Duc de Havré was one of their captains, riding in the royal carriage.
quote: surrounded by a squadron of the bodyguard

text: A triumphal arch of Louis XIV on the boulevards, and the popular theatre beside it, home of melodrama. From the boulevard the coaches for the eastern suburbs left from inns in the nearby alleys.
quote: the theatre of the Porte Saint-Martin

text: A silver one-franc coin, worth more than the lost fifteen sous; Madame Thénardier notices and keeps quiet. A night's lodging at the inn was normally twenty sous.
quote: it was a twenty-sou piece

text: 'Good fellow' or 'my good man', the patronising way of speaking to a working man or a beggar. The switch to 'Monsieur' marks Madame Thénardier's change of mind about her guest's purse.
quote: brave homme or bonhomme

text: Latin legal term, 'the body of the crime': the object or evidence proving that an offence was committed. Hugo applies it with mock solemnity to the Thénardier girls' doll.
quote: the corpus delicti

text: The widow of the murdered Duc de Berry and mother of the Bourbons' young heir, a celebrated figure at court. Saying 'Your Majesty' to her is Madame Thénardier's idea of absurd deference.
quote: as though to the Duchesse de Berry!

text: A liberal opposition newspaper of the Restoration. Thénardier reading it, three times over, fits his pose as a Bonapartist and liberal.
quote: began to read the Courrier Français

text: On Christmas eve French children set a shoe on the hearth for the Christ Child, or a 'good fairy', to fill with a small present or coin by morning. A ten-sou piece was a modest gift; a gold louis would be a fortune.
quote: children place their shoes in the chimney on Christmas eve

text: Brides wore a wreath of orange blossom, real or wax, a symbol of purity, and kept it afterwards under a glass globe on the mantelpiece. Thénardier has bought one second-hand for show.
quote: a woman’s headdress in silver wire and orange flowers

text: The 'centimes additionnels', surcharges added to direct taxes to fund local government, alongside the trade licence (patente) and the door and window tax. Madame Thénardier lists them all to plead poverty.
quote: the door and window tax, the hundredths!

text: Lord Castlereagh, the British foreign secretary who negotiated the peace settlement and the indemnity France had to pay the allies after 1815. Hugo compares Thénardier's dissatisfaction with his bill to his.
quote: the accent of Castlereagh auditing France’s bill

text: Gold twenty-franc coins struck under Louis XVIII bore his bare head with a short tied-back queue in place of Napoleon's laurel wreath. Hugo calls it 'Prussian', a sneer at a king restored by foreign armies.
quote: perfectly new twenty-franc pieces of the Restoration

text: Black clothes were worn for a set period after a death in the family, by children as well as adults. A child walking out of the village all in black is plainly mourning someone.
quote: a little girl dressed in mourning

text: Villages north of Montfermeil on the way back toward Paris, at the edge of the great forest of Bondy, long known for its highwaymen. The aqueduct of the old Abbey of Chelles crossed the woods there.
quote: in the direction of Livry and Bondy

text: A headland across the harbour from Toulon, with Cape Brun on the other side of the roadstead. Hugo names real places along an escaped convict's route, and a house that served as a 'dressing-room' where fugitives exchanged their convict red for ordinary clothes.
quote: in the neighborhood of Balaguier

text: One of the toll gates in the customs wall round Paris, on the north-west side. Entering the city there and crossing it by cab to the Observatoire, then on foot through the poor streets of the Ourcine and the Glacière, made the route hard to follow.
quote: by way of the Barrier Monceaux
